(

1 ) Osteoporotic fractures are a major cause of morbidity, decreased quality of life, and increased mortality worldwide. ( 2 , 3 , 4 ) For postmenopausal women (PMW), antiresorptive agents are usually the first‐line treatment and include bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate, zoledronate, or ibandronate) or denosumab. ( 5 , 6 ) Alendronate 70 mg tablet once weekly is the most commonly used bisphosphonate. Although alendronate has been shown to reduce the risk of vertebral, non‐vertebral, and hip fractures by 55%, 64%, and 47%, respectively, ( 7 ) adherence is problematic, with >50% discontinuing treatment within the first year. ( 8 , 9 )

Upper gastrointestinal (GI) side effects are one of the main reasons for discontinuing bisphosphonate treatment, observed in both real‐life studies ( 10 , 11 , 12 ) and clinical trials, ( 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ) resulting in reduced anti‐fracture efficacy and increased health care costs. ( 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 ) The International Osteoporosis Foundation and the European Calcified Tissue Society recognize the challenges with adherence associated with oral bisphosphonates. ( 21 )

In randomized clinical trials, the incidence of upper GI side effects in PMW treated with standard alendronate tablets (standard formulation) range from 20% to 30%, with similar incidence obtained for comparator groups in these trials. ( 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ) These values remain high, necessitating alternative therapeutic approaches. To address this, Binosto®, a novel buffered soluble alendronate 70 mg effervescent tablet formulation (ALN‐EFF), was specifically developed to improve GI tolerability through its effervescent formulation that has strong buffering properties. ( 22 , 23

) It provides a more convenient formulation to facilitate compliance, particularly in patients having difficulty swallowing tablets. ALN‐EFF is ingested as a buffered solution of fully dissolved alendronate to prevent the pH of gastric juice from further decreasing in the presence of alendronate, diminishing potential damage in cases of esophageal reflux and preventing contact of solid alendronate with the esophageal mucosa. ( 5 )

It has to be taken at least 30 minutes before the first meal of the day to permit adequate absorption. The effervescent tablet should be fully dissolved in plain water (≥120 mL) before consumption. This is to minimize esophageal irritation and esophageal toxicity as well as interactions with food items that limit the absorption of alendronate. ALN‐EFF is bioequivalent to Fosamax and was approved as a hybrid medicine in 2011 in the European Union and by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2012. ( 23 , 24 )
The aim of this study was to investigate the incidence of upper GI adverse events (AEs; (esophageal toxicity, gastritis, gastric ulcers, and duodenitis) and medication errors associated with ALN‐EFF.

2 Subjects and Methods 2.1 Study design This was a prospective, observational, multicenter, multinational, single‐arm, postauthorization safety study (PASS) to evaluate the incidence of upper GI AEs and medication errors during 12 months of treatment with ALN‐EFF. This study was registered on The European Union electronic Register of Post‐Authorisation Studies (EU PAS Register): ENCEPP/SDPP/10888. Patients were enrolled from primary and secondary care centers in Spain (16 centers) and Italy (7 centers) from May 2017 to February 2020.

The mean (±SD) follow‐up period was 12 ± 3 months with data collection time points at baseline, up to 2 months (“early” follow‐up), 2 to 9 months (“intermediate” follow‐up), and 9 to 15 months (“late” follow‐up) after baseline. Patients were followed from the date of the first prescription of ALN‐EFF (defined as index date). The occurrence of upper GI AEs (ie, including esophageal toxicity, gastritis, gastric ulcers, and duodenitis) was identified at routine visits during this period. Only AEs occurring within 12 ± 3 months of the index date were considered eligible.

At baseline, demographic data and levels of serum calcium were collected along with medical history about osteoporosis, fractures, and history of GI symptoms, as well as prior and concomitant treatment. The study was designed, conducted, and reported in accordance with the ethical principles laid down in the Declaration of Helsinki, the Good Pharmacoepidemiology Practices guidelines of the International Society for Pharmacoepidemiology, and applicable local rules and regulations. The protocol was approved by the Medicines and Healthcare Regulatory Authority in the UK.

2.2 Patient selection and eligibility criteria PMW were offered the possibility to participate in the study at the discretion of the treating physician only after the decision to prescribe ALN‐EFF for the treatment of osteoporosis was made. Patient selection was performed during routine clinical practice by the physician in accordance with ALN‐EFF product information. ( 22 )

Inclusion criteria were patients newly prescribed ALN‐EFF and naïve to bisphosphonate therapy; women with osteoporosis; written informed consent; and the ability to comply with the requirements of the study. Patients with a history of upper GI symptoms were also included. Exclusion criteria were the presence of any contraindications to ALN‐EFF according to Summary of Product Characteristics (SmPC). ( 22 , 23 )

2.3 Study objectives The primary objective of this study was to assess the cumulative incidence of upper GI AEs (esophageal toxicity, gastritis, gastric ulcers, and duodenitis) with ALN‐EFF, and the co‐primary objective was to assess the incidence of medication errors during treatment. Secondary aims were to evaluate persistence, discontinuation and reasons for discontinuation, and compliance with the SmPC recommendations for ALN‐EFF ( 22 , 23 ) and to calculate the incidence rate of ALN‐EFF individual gastric AEs. We also evaluated the association of a range of clinical characteristics (determinants) on the cumulative incidence of upper GI AEs with ALN‐EFF.

2.4 Outcome measures During follow‐up visits, information on AEs, medication errors (capture potential errors in the method of administration via questionnaire; Supplemental Table Table S1 ), and treatment discontinuation were collected. The following AEs were coded by MedDRA version 20.0 ( 25

) using preferred terms (PTs) that encompassed the primary endpoint for analysis of the cumulative incidence of upper GI AEs: esophagitis, esophageal ulcer, esophageal perforation, esophageal bleeding (PT: esophageal hemorrhage), esophageal stricture (PT: esophageal stenosis), gastritis, gastric ulcer, gastric perforation, gastric bleeding (PT: gastric hemorrhage), gastric stricture (PT: gastric stenosis), duodenitis, duodenal ulcer, duodenal perforation, duodenal bleeding (PT: small intestinal hemorrhage), duodenal stricture (PT: duodenal stenosis), and melaena. The presence of serious AEs (defined as an adverse reaction that results in death, is life‐threatening, requires hospitalization or prolongation of existing hospitalization, results in persistent or significant disability or incapacity, or is a birth defect) were also recorded.

In addition, other PTs were also analyzed within the primary endpoint of upper GI AEs (defined above) as they were considered potentially consistent with esophageal toxicity, gastritis, gastric ulcers, and duodenitis. These included abdominal pain, upper abdominal pain, dyspepsia, gastroesophageal reflux disease, nausea, abdominal distension, dysphagia, Helicobacter gastritis, Helicobacter infection, vomiting, and esophageal pain. Compliance was assessed using the Morisky‐Green 4‐question scale ( 26 ) and the number of tablets missed since the previous visit.

2.5 Statistical analysis A total of 1200 PMW with osteoporosis were planned to be enrolled to achieve 1000 evaluable patients allowing a precision (95% confidence intervals CIs]) of ±1% if the observed incidence of upper GI AEs is approximately 2%.

Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) for continuous variables and number and % for categorical variables. The cumulative incidence (proportion) of primary and secondary endpoints was calculated along with respective 95% CIs. The proportion (and 95% CIs) of subjects with medication errors was calculated. Persistence/discontinuation was analyzed using Kaplan–Meier curves and life tables. Multivariate logistic regression models were used to explore predictor variables influencing the occurrence of upper GI AEs related to ALN‐EFF, expressed as odds ratios (OR) and respective 95% CIs. Compliance using the Morisky‐Green score and tablet count are reported as mean scores (out of 100) ± SD. Where comparisons were made, quoted p values are two‐tailed and a value of p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Missing values were described with no imputation. All analyses were performed using SAS version 9.4 and SAS Enterprise Guide, version 7.1 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC, USA).

3 Results 3.1 Patient disposition and baseline characteristics A total of 1120 patients were screened and 1085 were eligible to participate in the study. Thirty‐five were excluded (13 did not fulfill inclusion criteria for patients newly prescribed ALN‐EFF and naïve to bisphosphonate therapy and 22 patients were excluded due to off‐label use) and 1 patient was not enrolled. A further 40 patients were excluded from analysis after enrollment because they did not take the study drug and 16 did not perform any follow‐up visits. Of the 1028 evaluable patients (646 from 16 centers in Spain ranging from 1 to 89 patients and 382 from seven centers in Italy ranging from 3 to 146 patients), 873 completed the 12 ± 3‐month follow‐up visit, and 155 patients did not complete all follow‐up visits, 2 died, and 3 withdrew consent (Fig. 1 ). These 1028 patients represented the Safety Set considered in this analysis.

Baseline clinical characteristics for all 1028 PMW are summarized in Table 1 . A total of 646 (62.8%) participated from 17 centers in Spain, and the remaining 382 (37.2%) from seven centers in Italy. Mean age was 67 ± 9 years and age at menopause was 49 ± 5 years. Just over one‐third ( n = 370; 36%) of patients had a previous fracture, the most frequent being vertebral ( n = 197; 53.2%) and 856 patients (83.3%) had at least one comorbid disease. 319 (31%) patients had a history of GI symptoms of which 271 (85%) were upper GI symptoms, the most frequent being dyspepsia ( n = 108; 33.9%) and gastritis ( n = 103; 32.3%). While all patients were naïve to bisphosphonates, 111 (10.8%) had previously received another treatment for osteoporosis (Table 2 ). The majority of patients enrolled in the study were receiving vitamin D and/or calcium supplementation (cholecalciferol [ n = 545, 87.2%] and/or calcium [ n = 260; 41.6%]) and 724 (70.4%) patients were receiving medication to treat other comorbidities. These were mainly antihypertensives ( n = 402, 55.5%) anti‐inflammatories ( n = 204, 28.2%), antidepressants ( n = 171, 23.6%), statins ( n = 169, 23.3%), and proton‐pump inhibitors ( n = 95, 13.1%).

The cumulative incidence of all upper GI AEs over the study period was 12.7% (95% CI 10.8–14.9%), whereas the cumulative incidence of upper GI AEs related to ALN‐EFF was 9.6% (CI 7.9–11.6%) (Fig. 2 ). Of these, 82 (8%; CI 6.4–9.8%) were of mild intensity, 15 (1.5%; CI 0.8–2.4%) of moderate intensity, and 2 (0.2%; CI 0.0–0.7%) of severe intensity (Table 3 ). The percentage of upper GI AEs related to ALN‐EFF reported at each visit decreased over the follow‐up period (Table 3 ). No serious upper GI AEs related to ALN‐EFF were reported over the entire study period. The most common upper GI AEs (≥1% of patients) related to ALN‐EFF were dyspepsia (2.7%; 28/1028), gastroesophageal reflux disease (2.4%; 25/1028), nausea (2.2%; 23/1028), and abdominal pain (1.3%; 13/1028). There were a total of 10 upper GI AEs that were considered by investigators to be related to ALN‐EFF with a cumulative incidence of <1%: gastritis (0.9%; 9/1028), all mild intensity; and duodenal ulcer (0.1%; 1/1028), of mild intensity on the background of a preexisting duodenal ulcer (“duodenal ulcer aggravated”). The incidence of specific upper GI AEs over the follow‐up period is shown in Fig. 3 . The majority of events were mild at the early follow‐up and intermediate follow‐up, decreasing at the late follow‐up for all four upper GI AEs. There were no reports of any of the following AEs: esophagitis, esophageal ulcer, esophageal perforation, esophageal hemorrhage, esophageal stenosis, gastric ulcer, gastric perforation, gastric hemorrhage, gastric stenosis, duodenitis, duodenal perforation, small intestine hemorrhage, duodenal stenosis, or melaena.

A range of individual baseline characteristics were found to be associated with upper GI AEs using univariate analysis (Supplemental Table S2 ). After multivariate adjustment, only country (Italy had higher levels than Spain) with an odds ratio (OR) = 4.5 (CI 2.8–7.2%), history of dyspepsia with OR = 3.1 (CI 1.6–5.9%), history of gastritis with OR = 2.9 (CI 1.7–5.2%), and history of concomitant medication with OR = 1.8 (CI 1.1–3.1%) remained significant determinants of upper GI AEs. The high OR for Italy was attributed to one site that reported a high incidence of AEs, upper GI AEs, and other AEs. 3.4 Incidence of individual gastric AEs

The incidence of ALN‐EFF individual gastric AEs was low as shown in Table 4 . The overall incidence rates (per 1000 patients/month) were 2.1 (CI 1.4–3.2) for nausea, 1.2 (CI 0.6–2.1) for abdominal pain, and 0.8 (CI 0.4–1.6) for gastritis (Table 4 ). The incidence rate also decreased over the three follow‐up periods for these three AEs. No events for gastric ulcer, gastric perforation, gastric hemorrhage, and gastric stenosis occurred. 3.5 Medication errors A total of 307 of 1028 patients (29.9%; CI 27.1–32.8%) made at least one medication error during the study with a total of 887 medication errors. The mean number of medication errors across all evaluable 1028 patients was 0.9 ± 7. From 1028 evaluable patients, 9.34% (CI 7.6–11.3%) made errors in the liquid used for dissolution (other liquid than plain water) and 0.97% (CI 0.5–1.8%) of patients in the volume of dissolution (<120 mL), 10.3% (CI 8.5–12.3%) made errors in the “waiting time before first meal” (intake of ALN‐EFF less than 30 minutes before the first meal of the day), 7.6% (CI 6.0–9.4%) made post‐administration drinking errors (not drinking at least 30 mL of plain water immediately after intake of the solution), 1.7% (CI 1.0–2.6%) made errors in the dosage (once weekly), 1.3% (CI 0.7–2.2%) made post‐administration behavior errors (stay upright less than 30′ after intake), 0.6% (6/1028; CI 0.2–1.3%) made errors in the complete dissolution of the preparation, and 0.1% (1/1028; CI 0.0–0.5%) used no liquid for dissolution. The majority of medication errors were associated with administration instructions applicable to any oral bisphosphonates in general (volume of liquid, 30 minutes before first meal, staying upright). Only seven medication errors were associated with an administration error specific to ALN‐EFF (six did not wait for the full dissolution of the preparation and one did not use liquid). Four medications errors were associated with AEs, three related to ALN‐EFF (two acid regurgitation and one gastritis of mild severity, non‐serious, with full recovery and continuation of ALN‐EFF). The third AE consisted of nausea of mild severity, non‐serious, related to ALN‐EFF, which resolved completely and reappeared upon administration of ALN‐EFF resulting in permanent discontinuation of ALN‐EFF. The number (and %) of patients making medication errors remained largely unchanged over the follow‐up period (Supplemental Table Table S3 ).

3.6 Discontinuation and compliance The mean time on ALN‐EFF was 12.8 months (CI 12.6–12.9). Of 1028 evaluable patients, 209 (20.3%) permanently discontinued ALN‐EFF over the follow‐up period. Discontinuation decreased steadily over time; 9.6% at 3 months, 6.0% at 6 months, 4.1% at 9 months, 2.4% at 12 months, and 2.3% at 15 months (Fig. 4 ). The most common reasons were AEs related to ALN‐EFF (46.9%; 98/209) and patient decision (42.6%; 89/209). Discontinuation for other causes constituted 24.9% (52/209) and 0.5% (1/209) were due to lack of efficacy. Among the 52 patients who discontinued for other causes, 14 (26.9%) discontinued due to dental care, 11 (21.2%) due to shortage of drug supplies, 8 (15.4%) for changes in treatment, 7 (13.5%) due to medical advice, 7 (13.5%) for other concomitant conditions, 4 (7.7%) due to patient condition, and 1 (1.9%) for other treatment issues. Multivariate logistic regression found age to be associated with discontinuation of ALN‐EFF due to AEs (OR = 0.96; CI 0.94–1.00).

The mean overall compliance using the Morisky‐Green questionnaire was 92.8 ± 8.6 and the mean overall compliance based on the number of tablets missed was 94.8 ± 8.1. Patient compliance did not change over the follow‐up period (Supplemental Table Table S4 ).

Multivariate logistic regression found that the only variables to be associated with treatment compliance with ALN‐EFF were country (improved compliance in Italy versus Spain; OR = 1.66; CI 1.2–2.4) and less compliance in patients with a history of GI symptoms (OR = 0.67; CI 0.5–1.0). Patient satisfaction remained high (approximately 90%) in terms of how easy it was to take ALN‐EFF and how much easier it was to take compared with other medications (Supplemental Table Table S5 ).

3.7 Reasons for discontinuation over the follow‐up period The most frequent reason for discontinuation, the presence of AEs, decreased over the follow‐up period, 38/53 patients (71.7%) at the early follow‐up, 45/71 patients (52.9%) at the intermediate follow‐up, and 15/98 patients (21.1%) at the late follow‐up. Only one patient discontinued due to lack of efficacy (at the late follow‐up visit) (Supplemental Table S6 ).

4 Discussion This postauthorization safety study (PASS) evaluated the incidence of upper GI AEs and medication errors of a novel buffered soluble alendronate 70 mg effervescent tablet formulation (ALN‐EFF) in PMW over 1 year in Italy and Spain. Results from this study provide evidence for the safe real‐world use of ALN‐EFF in bisphosphonate‐naïve PMW with osteoporosis. A total of 23% of patients experienced at least one AE during the study, while only 12.5% of patients reported AEs that were deemed to be related to ALN‐EFF. The incidence of AEs was similar to another real‐life experience with oral bisphosphonates. ( 27

) In addition, only a few AEs were serious, and no serious AE were related to ALN‐EFF. The vast majority (96%) of AEs related to ALN‐EFF were of mild or moderate intensity, and a high level of satisfaction with taking ALN‐EFF was found at both early and late follow‐up. The cumulative incidence of all upper GI AEs during this 1‐year study was 12.7%, with the majority of these (9.6%) considered to be related to ALN‐EFF. Upper GI AEs related to ALN‐EFF decreased with time and were almost all of mild‐to‐moderate intensity with only two judged as severe, both of brief duration with full patient recovery.

These results cannot directly be compared with other studies because of the lack of a control group and potential differences in the patient population (baseline characteristics) from other studies. However, the incidence of upper GI AEs in this “real‐world” study were found to be lower than that observed in alendronate‐treated groups from randomized controlled trials with a duration of 12 months. In the FIT study (5 mg ALN daily in the first 2 years, then 10 mg/d), the incidence in the first 12 months was about 30%. ( 13 ) In a second 12‐month trial using a dose of 10 mg/d, the incidence was 21.3% over 12 months. ( 14

) Two further trials that continued 70 mg once weekly for at least 1 year (ie, similar to ALN‐EFF) with incidence of upper GI AEs of 23.5% ( 16 ) in one and 22.5% ( 15 ) in the other. A 3‐month safety study of 70 mg once weekly reported an incidence of 11% over 3 months. ( 28 ) This evidence is consistent with the conclusion that the ALN‐EFF dosing regimen may result in lower incidence of upper GI events over 1 year than a pill at the same dose.

The incidence of more concerning upper GI events (ie, ulcer, perforation, hemorrhage, stenosis, etc.) were not reported. In this regard, the physician would have certainly prescribed an esophagogastroduodenoscopy in cases where the patients would have presented severe clinical symptoms. At least one medication error occurred in 29.9% of patients and only seven medication errors were associated with an administration error specific to the new ALN‐EFF formulation, while the vast majority of administration errors in medication observed were common to the administration procedure for any oral bisphosphonate. ( 29

) In this regard, Ettinger and colleagues reported in an analysis of 812 women that around 60% did not comply with at least one of the alendronate dosing instructions, mostly waiting 30 minutes before food and using liquid other than water. These two dosing instruction errors were observed in two‐thirds of patients reporting medication errors. ( 29

) However, the results of our study show that the use of the ALN‐EFF‐specific alendronate formulation is not associated with an increased risk of medication errors compared with standard oral alendronate formulations. It is recognized that instructions for proper administration of bisphosphonates are rather complex and require adequate education from health care professionals to patients, particularly in elderly people. ( 30 )

Only 4 patients reported AEs associated with medication errors, which were of mild severity, non‐serious, and all recovered. Only in one case did this lead to discontinuation of ALN‐EFF. Improper administration (correct amount of water or staying in upright position for 30′) of alendronate has been associated with esophageal mucosal injury, especially in post marketing reports. ( 10 , 13 ) This was not observed in this study of more than 1000 patients. The incidence of ALN‐EFF individual gastric AEs was low, ranging from 0% to 2.1% per 1000 patients/month. Large prescription‐event monitoring studies have been carried out in England for alendronate in PMW with osteoporosis. ( 31 , 32

) In the first study involving 1523 patients, 20 (1.3%) experienced an esophageal event that was possibly related to alendronate. ( 31 ) In the second study, involving 11,916 patients, the incidence density for the overall treatment period (IDA) for dyspeptic conditions was 10.1 per 1000 patients/month, nausea and vomiting 4.8 per 1000 patients/months, and abdominal pain 3.8 per 1000 patients/month. ( 32

) Based on these studies, a report commissioned by the UK National Health Service concluded that conventional alendronate appeared to be associated with GI complaints but with some degree of uncertainty due to the lack of a placebo arm. Despite the absence of a direct comparison between these ALN‐EFF study results, the IDA for nausea and vomiting and abdominal pain appeared to be lower for ALN‐EFF. It is recognized that approximately three‐quarters of women who initiate bisphosphonates are nonadherent to treatment and almost 50% discontinue therapy within the first year. ( 8 , 9

) For ALN‐EFF, a lower discontinuation was observed in this study, with approximately one‐fifth (20.3%) of patients permanently discontinuing treatment. The decline in discontinuation in the first month was larger followed by a time‐dependent steady decline thereafter. This supports the observation that people who have problems with tolerability or experience early side effects tend to stop treatment early. The interpretation of these results is in line with previous publications where patients who interrupt therapy with bisphosphonates do so because of drug‐induced AEs. Undoubtedly, among these AEs, those affecting the upper GI system are by far the most frequent. ( 9

) Nonetheless, the comparably lower discontinuation rate due to tolerability and AEs may be the best indicator of the real‐world experience of ALN‐EFF in this study. After multivariable adjustment, only history of dyspepsia, history of gastritis, and history of concomitant medication remained as significant determinants of upper GI events. These results are consistent with other studies, ( 13

) where previous upper GI tract disease was identified as an important independent risk factor for upper GI tract events. Though the perception is that alendronate frequently causes GI tract intolerance, it is likely that upper GI complaints are common among elderly women, as observed in the FIT study, (13 ) regardless of alendronate treatment or placebo. In addition, differences in results between Spain and Italy may indicate cultural differences and health care system can affect the reporting of AEs. Nonetheless, the results of this analysis should be applicable to a wide range of PMW with osteoporosis who are naïve to bisphosphonates according to the SmPC.
To date, only one study has evaluated the effect of ALN‐EFF compared with standard ALN tablets on bone mineral density (BMD) and bone‐alkaline phosphatase (b‐ALP). ( 33

) A preliminary study by Giusti and colleagues involving 42 PMW with BMD T ‐score <−2.5 (or between −2 and −2.5 and at least one vertebral fracture) were treated with ALN‐EX for 12 months and compared with 54 PMW on alendronate standard tablet randomly selected from a historical cohort. After 12 months of treatment, the two groups showed a similar increase in femoral neck and total hip BMD. The absolute decrease (mean U/L ± SD) of b‐ALP was also comparable between the ALN‐EX group (−6.0 ± 2.8 U/L) and the standard alendronate group (−6.9 ± 4.4 U/L). These preliminary results demonstrated that ALN‐EFF is as effective as traditional alendronate tablet on surrogate anti‐fracture efficacy outcomes.

4.1 Study strengths The strengths of the present study are that this was a real‐world assessment of upper GI AEs in a wide variety of clinical settings in a large number ( N = 1028) of PMW in two EU countries. Although participating physicians may not be representative of all physicians who were prescribing ALN‐EFF, the wide spectrum of sites (primary and secondary care centers) and consecutive recruitment of eligible patients minimized any systematic selection bias and may permit generalizability of the results to populations in Spain and Italy.

Medication errors were assessed in routine clinical practice and reasons for discontinuation of ALN‐EFF were systematically assessed. At baseline, 31% of enrolled patients reported a medical history of GI tract conditions that did not exclude study participation, and 85% of these patients presented with a history of upper GI symptoms. The limited exclusion criteria may be a better reflection of real‐world experience with ALN‐EFF compared with previous clinical studies with oral alendronates with more restrictive exclusion criteria. ( 34 )

This observational (PASS) design separated the prescription from the decision to include a patient in the study, followed current clinical practice, and allows for the inclusion of a wide range of patients who used ALN‐EFF. 4.2 Study limitations The main limitation of the present study was the lack of a control group with weekly 70 mg alendronate in a similar real‐world setting to compare the incidence of upper GI AEs, persistence, and discontinuation with ALN‐EFF. Events observed were symptomatic AEs, with any further investigation determined as necessary during routine clinical practice.

Loss to follow‐up was different between Italy and Spain according to different clinical practice in the two countries and due to differences in the wording of the country‐specific case report forms. Data collection on the intensity of AEs was requested after recruitment and data collection had already started, so data were not available for all patients enrolled. Assessment of adherence was limited in patients recorded as having temporary discontinuations of treatment.

The small number of patients and events in some patient subgroups meant that the assessment of many secondary and exploratory objectives was limited. Therefore, results derived from some of these subgroup analyses need to be interpreted with caution.

Conclusion Based on the results of this study, it is suggested that ALN‐EFF may represent an alendronate treatment for patients with postmenopausal osteoporosis that is associated with preferable pharmacologic properties translating into clinical benefit for patients. Many of the upper GI AEs of interest (primary objective) were observed to occur at a lower incidence compared with the reported frequency from randomized controlled trials and post‐marketing data in the SmPC of the reference product (alendronate tablets). ( 35 ) Furthermore, ALN‐EFF was not associated with a detectable increase in the risk of serious upper GI tract AEs.

This PASS was initiated in order to generate real‐world data on this new formulation of alendronate, a buffered, oral solution. The results provide evidence that ALN‐EFF does not lead to a higher incidence of upper GI/esophageal AEs compared with standard alendronate tablets and despite its somewhat different mode of preparation/administration versus standard alendronate tablets does not lead to an increased incidence of administration errors.

Further studies beyond 12 months to determine whether persistence can be maintained and whether increased persistence translates into improved long‐term efficacy (eg, increase in bone mineral disease, incidence of secondary fractures, etc.) are warranted. Finally, having a drug with negligible side effects allows long‐term adherence. This is of utmost importance in a pandemic period in which patients are reluctant to go to hospitals or to outpatient clinics.

Over 100 medications have been implicated in inducing direct mucosal injury, including tetracyclines, bisphosphonates, potassium chloride, ferrous sulphate, and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs [ 1 , 2 ]. Doxycycline is a second-generation tetracycline typically prescribed for acne, rosacea, and sexually transmitted infections [ 3 - 5 ]. Pill oesophagitis is characterised by abrupt retrosternal pain and odynophagia with or without dysphagia shortly after ingestion of medication [ 1 ]. Injury commonly affects the mid-oesophagus, where extrinsic compression from the aortic arch or left main bronchus may predispose to tablet retention [ 6 - 8 ]. Endoscopic findings typically include focal erythema, erosions, “kissing” ulcers, bleeding ulcers, or, rarely, strictures [ 6 ].

This case report aims to highlight the potential for doxycycline-induced oesophagitis to cause severe circumferential oesophageal injury requiring prolonged hospitalisation, multidisciplinary management, and investigation to exclude life-threatening complications. It also seeks to emphasise the importance of early recognition, timely endoscopic assessment, and effective conservative management in a regional Australian hospital, alongside preventative prescribing practices.

Case presentation A 32-year-old Australian-born woman presented to a rural emergency department with four days of retrosternal pain and foreign-body sensation. She reported pain at rest and severe odynophagia limiting oral intake. She had commenced oral doxycycline, 100 mg slow-release capsule daily, for rosacea seven days earlier. Her relevant history included endometriosis, irritable bowel syndrome, and a previous laparoscopic cholecystectomy. She underwent an unremarkable gastroscopy and colonoscopy six years ago. She took no other medications, was a non-smoker, and rarely consumed alcohol. On examination, there was mild epigastric tenderness, and she remained haemodynamically stable.

Initial blood tests demonstrated mild leukocytosis (11.4 × 10 9 /L) with neutrophilia (8.39 × 10 9 /L); serum lipase, liver function tests, and serial troponins were unremarkable (Table 1 ). Chest radiograph and serial electrocardiography traces were normal. Table 1 Initial serum investigation results on presentation. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen with oral contrast showed mild wall thickening in the middle third of the oesophagus without extraluminal leak or mediastinal free air (Figures 1A , 1B ).

Within 24 hours of presentation, she underwent an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy which demonstrated localised circumferential erosions in the middle third of the oesophagus (Figures 2A , 2B ). The gastro-oesophageal junction was anatomically preserved, with a regular Z-line identified 34 cm from the incisors. Bilious fluid was observed within the stomach; however, the gastric cardia and fundus appeared normal on retroflexion, and the examined duodenum was unremarkable. Cold-forceps biopsies were obtained directly from the oesophageal lesion for histopathological and microbiological examination. The procedure was completed without immediate complications. Histopathology from the mid-oesophageal biopsy demonstrated ulcerative oesophagitis with granulomatous inflammation. There was no dysplasia, malignancy, viral inclusions, or foreign material. Immunostains for cytomegalovirus and herpes simplex virus were negative. She was commenced on an oral sucralfate suspension 1 g four times daily for one week.

With regular dietitian input, her diet was advanced to free fluids on day five, then soft diet on day seven of admission. By day eight, she was pain-free and discharged with oral pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily and instructed to remain upright during oral intake. She remained clinically well in the community, and repeat upper gastrointestinal endoscopy two months after the index admission demonstrated a normal oesophagus, stomach, and duodenum (Figures 3A , 3B ).

Discussion Large clinical series have shown that pill oesophagitis commonly presents with chest pain, odynophagia, dysphagia, vomiting, haematemesis, and melaena [ 6 , 9 ]. In Kim et al.’s 78-patient series, 78.2% of lesions were located in the middle third of the oesophagus [ 9 ]. Endoscopic findings in that cohort were usually ulceration or erosion, consistent with the present case [ 9 ]. Doxycycline is repeatedly identified as a leading cause of pill oesophagitis. Al-Mofarreh and Al Mofleh reported 36 cases of oesophageal ulceration complicating doxycycline therapy in a predominantly young population [ 10 ]. Kadayifci et al. described five cases of doxycycline-induced pill oesophagitis, all in young or middle-aged women, with mid-oesophageal injury and retrosternal pain or dysphagia [ 11 ]. More recent series in patients receiving doxycycline for acne have reinforced the same pattern of abrupt symptoms, mid-oesophageal ulceration, and recovery after cessation of the drug [ 12 ].

In this case, the patient had recently commenced doxycycline capsules containing modified-release pellets of doxycycline hyclate, coated to slow but not prevent release in acid media [ 13 ]. These gelatin-coated capsules are likely more adherent to the oesophagus than similarly sized tablets, causing premature release of their contents [ 7 ]. This proposed mechanism of prolonged mucosal contact by the offending medication is exacerbated when ingested with insufficient water or immediately before lying down [ 1 , 6 ]. Doxycycline has acidic properties when dissolved locally, which may explain its capacity to produce sharply demarcated erosive or ulcerative injury [ 6 ]. The mid-oesophagus is vulnerable because of anatomical narrowing and extrinsic compression by the aortic arch and left main bronchus. Accounting for this, preventative education should include instructions to swallow pills with adequate water, remain upright after ingestion, and avoid lying down for at least 30 minutes.

Immediate management involves cessation of offending medication. Acid suppression is commonly used to reduce secondary reflux-mediated injury and assist symptom control. Sucralfate is intended to provide a protective mucosal barrier. Intravenous fluids, antiemetics, and multimodal analgesia are useful adjuncts if pain precludes adequate oral intake. Severe persistent retrosternal pain can raise concern for perforation or mediastinitis. In this case, endoscopy confirmed partial-thickness mucosal injury, while CT with oral contrast was reassuringly negative for leak, free air, and mediastinal collection. This permitted ongoing conservative management in a rural hospital.

Histopathology in pill-induced oesophagitis is often non-specific but helps exclude malignancy, infection, eosinophilic oesophagitis, and other inflammatory mimics [ 8 , 14 , 15 ]. Kim et al.’s histomorphological study described features that may favour pill-induced injury over reflux oesophagitis, including diffuse dilated intercellular spaces, intraepithelial pustules, eosinophilic microabscesses, and inflammatory infiltrates [ 15 ]. There are broad-ranging differential diagnoses for granulomatous oesophagitis, including infection (tuberculosis, fungal, viral), sarcoidosis, foreign-body reaction, eosinophilic oesophagitis, and malignancy. In our case, the apparent granulomatous inflammation was unusual but not accompanied by acid-fast bacilli, fungal elements, viral inclusions, dysplasia, or foreign material, supporting a reactive inflammatory process secondary to severe ulceration.

General surgeons frequently assess patients with acute dysphagia and chest or epigastric pain in rural settings where formal gastroenterology services are not immediately available. Recognition of medication-induced oesophageal injury, early endoscopic assessment, and multidisciplinary management are key to achieving favourable outcomes.

This report is limited by its single-case design, which restricts generalisability, and the absence of formal causality assessment, drug rechallenge, or analysis of doxycycline formulation and drug concentration. Diagnosis was supported by temporal association, characteristic endoscopic findings, and clinical resolution following drug cessation. Furthermore, management within a regional Australian hospital may have been influenced by resource limitations and access to subspecialty services, potentially affecting the applicability of these findings to other healthcare settings.

Conclusions Doxycycline-induced oesophagitis should be considered in the differential diagnosis of patients presenting with acute retrosternal pain and odynophagia following recent initiation of doxycycline therapy. Severe cases may clinically mimic oesophageal perforation or food bolus impaction, potentially leading to diagnostic uncertainty. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy plays a key role in establishing the diagnosis, evaluating the extent of mucosal injury, and excluding alternative oesophageal pathology. Early recognition and prompt discontinuation of the offending medication are essential for favourable clinical outcomes. Conservative management, including acid suppression, mucosal protection with sucralfate, and appropriate nutritional support, is generally effective. Furthermore, patient education regarding proper medication administration, particularly adequate water intake and remaining upright after ingestion, is crucial to preventing recurrence. This case highlights the importance of maintaining a high index of suspicion for medication-induced oesophageal injury to facilitate timely diagnosis, avoid unnecessary interventions, and optimise patient outcomes.

Background Drug-associated esophageal ulceration and perforation are uncommon but clinically serious adverse events. This study characterized post-marketing reporting patterns for these events across three spontaneous reporting systems.

Methods Reports from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS), Japanese Adverse Drug Event Report database (JADER), and Canada Vigilance from 2004 to 2025 were analyzed using predefined Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) preferred terms. Disproportionality was assessed using the reporting odds ratio (ROR), proportional reporting ratio (PRR), Bayesian confidence propagation neural network (BCPNN), and multi-item gamma Poisson shrinker (MGPS). In FAERS, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression followed by multivariable logistic regression was used for exploratory signal prioritization. Reported time-to-onset was summarized for drug-report records with valid therapy start and event onset dates.

Results FAERS contained 8,061 reports meeting the prespecified composite case definition. Among the 50 most frequently reported FAERS primary-suspect drugs, the largest disproportionality estimates were observed for doxycycline (ROR 41.15, 95% confidence interval [CI] 36.47–46.43), alendronic acid (ROR 21.45, 95% CI 19.14–24.04), and clindamycin (ROR 18.59, 95% CI 15.40-22.44). JADER and Canada Vigilance showed descriptively overlapping but heterogeneous reporting patterns. Reported time-to-onset was heterogeneous, with both short and long recorded intervals.

Conclusions This multidatabase analysis identified prominent reporting signals for established pill-injury drugs and exploratory reporting patterns involving other drug categories. These findings are hypothesis-generating and should not be interpreted as estimates of incidence, comparative clinical risk, or causal effects. Its clinical spectrum ranges from transient esophagitis to ulceration, hemorrhage, stricture, rupture, and, in severe cases, esophageal perforation. Symptoms are often nonspecific, including retrosternal pain, odynophagia, dysphagia, heartburn-like symptoms, upper gastrointestinal bleeding, or acute chest discomfort. Because these presentations overlap with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), infectious esophagitis, malignancy-related symptoms, and treatment-related mucosal injury, drug-associated esophageal injury may be under-recognized in routine practice. This is particularly relevant for older adults, patients with dysphagia or impaired mobility, patients receiving multiple medications, and patients with cancer or organ transplantation who often have complex therapeutic exposures. Although many pill-related injuries are preventable through administration counseling, serious ulceration, hemorrhage, rupture, and perforation continue to be reported, making post-marketing signal detection clinically relevant [ 1 – 3 ].

Classic drug-induced esophageal injury is usually attributed to prolonged contact between a tablet or capsule and the esophageal mucosa. Contributing factors include insufficient water intake, recumbency shortly after administration, large pill size, caustic drug formulation, pre-existing esophageal motility disorder, dysphagia, advanced age, and structural esophageal disease [ 1 – 3 ]. Several drug classes have long-standing biological plausibility for esophageal mucosal injury. Bisphosphonates, especially alendronate, have been associated with characteristic endoscopic and pathological esophageal injury, particularly when administration instructions are not followed [ 4 ]. Doxycycline remains one of the best-recognized causes of pill-induced esophagitis and ulceration, with reports spanning classic case series, histopathologic descriptions, and recent case literature [ 5 – 9 ]. Clindamycin-induced esophageal injury may also be underdiagnosed because its symptoms can resemble reflux disease or infectious esophagitis [ 10 ]. Dabigatran represents a distinct example because its tartaric acid-containing capsule may contribute to local acidic mucosal injury, while systemic anticoagulation may worsen bleeding or delay mucosal recovery [ 11 , 12 ].

Contemporary prescribing patterns have broadened the clinical context of esophageal ulceration and perforation beyond classic pill retention [ 13 ]. Antiplatelet agents, anticoagulants, and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may not always act as direct caustic agents in the esophagus, but they may amplify bleeding, impair mucosal defense, or delay recovery once mucosal injury has occurred [ 14 – 16 ]. In immunosuppressed patients, esophageal ulceration may reflect drug-related mucosal injury, impaired mucosal repair, or opportunistic infection rather than a single direct toxic mechanism [ 17 , 18 ]. Mycophenolate-associated gastrointestinal mucosal injury has been described histologically [ 19 ]. Opportunistic infections such as cytomegalovirus can involve ulcerative esophageal disease in immunocompromised hosts [ 17 , 18 , 20 ]. In oncology practice, cytotoxic chemotherapy, targeted therapy, antiangiogenic therapy, and immune checkpoint inhibitors may coincide with mucosal inflammation, impaired tissue repair, infection susceptibility, tumor-related factors, or intensive diagnostic surveillance. Evidence on immune checkpoint inhibitor-related esophagitis supports clinical awareness but cannot be extrapolated directly to disproportionality estimates without clinical validation [ 21 ].

Spontaneous reporting systems provide an important opportunity to detect rare or unexpected adverse drug event signals after marketing approval. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS), Japanese Adverse Drug Event Report database (JADER), and Canada Vigilance collect reports from healthcare professionals, consumers, manufacturers, and regulatory sources. These systems are useful for identifying potential safety concerns involving rare but serious outcomes that are difficult to characterize in pre-approval trials. However, they are affected by underreporting, duplicate reporting, stimulated reporting, incomplete clinical information, selective reporting, regional differences in drug utilization, and the absence of exposure denominators [ 22 , 23 ]. Disproportionality analyses therefore cannot estimate incidence, absolute risk, or causality. These limitations are particularly relevant for esophageal injury, where a drug may be reported because it treated pre-existing or prodromal symptoms. For example, proton pump inhibitor (PPI) signals may reflect GERD, erosive esophagitis, ulcer symptoms, or gastroprotection in patients receiving NSAIDs or antithrombotic agents, rather than direct PPI toxicity [ 14 – 16 , 24 , 25 ].

Previous evidence has clarified the clinical presentation, endoscopic features, mechanisms, and management of drug-induced esophageal injury, but the literature remains dominated by clinical reviews, case reports, and single-system pharmacovigilance designs [ 22 ]. Several gaps remain. First, evidence from different spontaneous reporting systems has rarely been considered together, making it difficult to understand whether signals are observed across different reporting environments. Second, most clinical discussions focus on classic local irritants, whereas signals involving antithrombotic agents, immunosuppressants, and antineoplastic therapies remain less systematically characterized. Third, time-to-onset information is often underused, although onset patterns may help distinguish early local irritation from more heterogeneous delayed reporting patterns. Fourth, patient-safety implications are not always clearly linked to pharmacovigilance findings.

The present study addressed these gaps using a multidatabase post-marketing pharmacovigilance approach [ 26 ]. Reports meeting a prespecified composite definition of esophageal ulceration- and perforation-related events were analyzed separately in FAERS, JADER, and Canada Vigilance from 2004 to 2025. Disproportionality analyses were used to identify reporting signals, while exploratory least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) and multivariable logistic regression analyses were used to prioritize selected FAERS drug-event pairs. Time-to-onset analyses described recorded temporal patterns among eligible drug-report records. The study was designed for descriptive comparison across reporting systems, not causal inference, incidence estimation, or formal external validation.

Materials and methods Study design and data sources This was a retrospective multidatabase pharmacovigilance study designed to identify post-marketing reporting signals for drug-associated esophageal ulceration and perforation. Three spontaneous reporting systems were analyzed: FAERS, JADER, and the Canada Vigilance Adverse Reaction Online Database. The study was conducted as a signal-detection and signal-prioritization analysis rather than a causal inference study. Therefore, all findings were interpreted as reporting associations rather than incidence rates, absolute risks, or confirmed causal relationships.

FAERS quarterly data files from the first quarter of 2004 through the first quarter of 2025 were downloaded and imported into PostgreSQL version 14.4. The following FAERS tables were used: DEMO (demographic and administrative information), DRUG (drug information), REAC (adverse-event terms), OUTC (patient outcomes), RPSR (report sources), THER (therapy dates), and INDI (reported indications). Reports were linked using the corresponding report identifiers. JADER and the Canada Vigilance Adverse Reaction Online Database were analyzed as additional spontaneous reporting systems for descriptive cross-database comparison. Adverse events were harmonized using Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) preferred terms where applicable.

Because FAERS, JADER, and Canada Vigilance are spontaneous reporting systems, the unit of analysis was the adverse event report rather than the exposed patient. The number of patients exposed to each drug was not available. Therefore, incidence rates, exposure-adjusted risks, and causal effects could not be calculated.

Deduplication and data cleaning Duplicate FAERS reports were removed according to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-recommended procedure. When multiple records shared the same FAERS case identifier (CASEID), the report with the most recent FDA receipt date (FDA_DT) was retained. If both CASEID and FDA_DT were identical, the record with the highest primary report identifier (PRIMARYID) was retained. Remaining duplicate PRIMARYID records were then removed.

Drug names were standardized to generic active ingredients where possible, with spelling variants, salt forms, and brand names harmonized when they referred to the same ingredient. Reporting country names were standardized to reduce duplicate categories. Age values outside 0-120 years and weight values greater than 400 kg were treated as implausible in analyses involving these variables. Missing demographic information was reported explicitly and was not imputed.

Case definition Terminology was defined to distinguish clinical entities from the analytical outcome. ‘Esophageal injury’ was used only as a broad clinical descriptor and was not a coded endpoint. The ulceration-related component comprised the MedDRA preferred terms ‘esophagitis ulcerative,’ ‘esophageal ulcer haemorrhage,’ ‘esophageal ulcer,’ ‘necrotising esophagitis,’ and ‘acute esophageal mucosal lesion.’ The perforation-related component comprised ‘esophageal ulcer perforation,’ ‘esophageal rupture,’ and ‘esophageal perforation.’

For the primary pharmacovigilance analyses, these eight preferred terms were combined into a composite outcome termed ‘esophageal ulceration- and perforation-related events.’ Pooling supported signal detection for rare related events but did not imply clinical, pathological, mechanistic, or severity equivalence. Drug-specific outcome- and severity-stratified disproportionality analyses were not performed. Reports were classified from coded preferred terms without independent clinical adjudication. Non-cases consisted of all other reports in the corresponding database during the same period; the FAERS primary analysis focused on drugs recorded as primary suspects.

Descriptive analysis of FAERS reports Descriptive analyses were performed for FAERS reports meeting the composite case definition. Baseline characteristics included age, sex, body weight, reporter occupation, reporting country, reporting quarter, and retained serious-outcome code. Categorical variables were summarized as counts and percentages, and missing values were retained as separate categories. Quarterly reporting trends, age distribution, and retained serious-outcome codes were visualized in Fig. 1 .

Disproportionality analysis in FAERS Disproportionality analyses evaluated whether individual primary-suspect drugs were reported disproportionately with the composite outcome relative to other reported outcomes. For each drug-composite-outcome comparison, a two-by-two contingency table was constructed: a = number of reports containing both the drug of interest and the composite outcome; b = number of reports containing the drug of interest and other outcomes; c = number of reports containing the composite outcome with other primary-suspect drugs; d = number of reports containing other primary-suspect drugs and other outcomes.

Four signal-detection algorithms were used: reporting odds ratio (ROR), proportional reporting ratio (PRR), Bayesian confidence propagation neural network (BCPNN), and multi-item gamma Poisson shrinker (MGPS) [ 27 – 32 ]. BCPNN was summarized by the information component (IC) and its lower credibility limit (IC025). For MGPS, openEBGM version 0.9.1 fitted a two-gamma-mixture prior across the 809 FAERS comparisons; the empirical Bayes geometric mean (EBGM) and its posterior 5th percentile (EBGM05) were reported. Formulas, fitted hyperparameters, and signal thresholds are provided in Supplementary Table S1 . Two-sided Fisher’s exact tests were used when any expected cell count was < 5; otherwise, two-sided Pearson chi-square tests were used. The multiplicity family comprised 809 FAERS primary-suspect drug-composite-outcome comparisons. Bonferroni-adjusted P values were calculated as min(809 × raw P, 1); thus, adjusted P < 0.01 corresponded to raw P < 1.236 × 10 -5 . Complete results are provided in Supplementary Table S2 .

The 50 primary-suspect drugs with the largest numbers of composite-outcome reports in FAERS were displayed in forest and volcano plots. These analyses were used for signal detection and prioritization only. ROR, PRR, BCPNN, and MGPS results were not interpreted as incidence rates, exposure-adjusted risks, or evidence of causality.

Exploratory signal prioritization using LASSO and multivariable logistic regression Candidate screening for LASSO was performed exclusively within FAERS and did not require a drug to appear in JADER or Canada Vigilance. Entry required all three prespecified criteria: more than 100 reports meeting the composite case definition, an ROR lower 95% confidence limit > 1, and a Bonferroni-adjusted P value < 0.01. Eleven of the 809 evaluated drug-composite-outcome comparisons met these criteria and entered LASSO.

The binomial LASSO analysis used the restricted report-level preprocessing object containing 3,120,039 reports, including 2,137 reports meeting the composite case definition. The model used alpha = 1, standardized predictors, a fixed random seed of 20,260,826, and outcome-stratified 10-fold cross-validation based on binomial deviance. The minimum-deviance criterion was selected (lambda.min = 1.128109 × 10 -5 ); lambda.1se was 6.607358 × 10 -5 . All 11 candidate drug indicators had nonzero coefficients at both penalty values and were carried forward to multivariable logistic regression. LASSO therefore did not reduce the prescreened set and was retained as an exploratory shrinkage step. In this object, candidate indicators were derived from one standardized primary-suspect DRUG value per report; a separate DrugList field retained all recorded drug entries and roles and was used for the PPI-exclusion analysis.

For multivariable logistic regression, 389 records with age values outside 0-120 years, including one report meeting the composite case definition, were excluded from the preprocessing object. The valid-age model therefore included 3,119,650 reports and 2,136 composite-outcome reports. The object was restricted to records with non-missing age and body weight, although body weight was not included in the model. Age and sex were included a priori; female and male indicators were compared with missing, unknown, or other sex. The resulting adjusted odds ratios are estimates from this FAERS case/non-case model and do not represent independent clinical risk factors or causal effects. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was calculated in the same sample as an apparent measure of discrimination; no internal or external model validation was performed.

Exploratory sensitivity and stratified analyses To assess PPI-related reporting context, an exploratory report-level sensitivity analysis was performed within the restricted regression-preprocessing object containing 3,120,039 reports, including 2,137 composite-outcome reports. The DrugList field was used to exclude reports containing esomeprazole, omeprazole, pantoprazole, lansoprazole, rabeprazole, or dexlansoprazole in any recorded drug role. The four disproportionality measures were recalculated for the 10 non-PPI candidates; MGPS priors were fitted across all primary-suspect drug comparisons in the restricted data before and after exclusion. This object is a restricted subset of the 18,937,868-report primary FAERS population, so the analysis evaluates stability only within that subset.

Age-stratified analysis used reports in the same object with valid ages from 0 to 120 years. Reports were classified as < 65 or ≥ 65 years. Stratum-specific RORs were calculated for the 11 candidate drugs, and heterogeneity was assessed with the ratio of the older-group ROR to the younger-group ROR. Heterogeneity P values were adjusted across 11 drug comparisons using the Benjamini-Hochberg method. A 0.5 continuity correction was applied only when a stratum-specific two-by-two table contained a zero cell. These analyses describe reporting heterogeneity, not age-specific incidence or susceptibility.

Cross-database signal comparison using JADER and Canada Vigilance Disproportionality analyses were conducted separately in JADER and Canada Vigilance using the same general case definition and signal-detection framework. JADER results were displayed for the 50 suspected-drug entries with the largest numbers of composite-outcome reports. The archived Canada Vigilance extract contained product-name-specific aggregate rows, so branded, biosimilar, and generic entries were retained separately. Because report-level identifiers were unavailable in this extract, aliases could not be deduplicated reliably and product-specific rows were not summed into ingredient-level totals.

Cross-database analysis was exploratory and descriptive. FAERS, JADER, and Canada Vigilance differ in database size, population coverage, reporting rules, regulatory context, drug utilization, reporter composition, and data completeness; their ROR magnitudes were therefore not compared directly. Recurrence was described as database-specific overlap that may increase priority for further study, not external validation. Absence of a signal in another database was not interpreted as evidence of no association.

Time-to-onset analysis Time-to-onset was calculated in FAERS as the interval between the reported therapy start date for a drug and the adverse-event onset date. Each eligible drug-report pair contributed one onset record; multiple drug-specific records could therefore arise from the same adverse-event report. Records with missing, incomplete, implausible, or negative intervals were excluded. Eligible onset records were summarized using medians and interquartile ranges (IQRs), grouped interval counts, and cumulative percentages.

Weibull analysis was performed for 37 drugs that met the ROR signal criterion among the 50 most frequently reported FAERS primary suspects and had available onset data. The scale parameter describes the time scale of the fitted recorded-onset distribution, whereas the shape parameter describes its temporal pattern. An upper 95% confidence limit for the shape parameter < 1 was classified as an early-failure pattern, a 95% confidence interval including 1 as a random-failure pattern, and a lower 95% confidence limit > 1 as a wear-out pattern [ 33 ]. Because scale and shape parameters are positive, their confidence intervals were calculated on the log scale.

Time-to-onset and Weibull findings were interpreted only as descriptions of recorded onset patterns. They do not estimate incidence, an exposure-based hazard, or a biological risk window because the data lack risk sets, censoring information, verified treatment timelines, and independence across drug-report records.

Bias considerations for proton pump inhibitor signals Proton pump inhibitor-related signals were interpreted cautiously. Drugs such as esomeprazole, omeprazole, and rabeprazole are frequently prescribed for gastroesophageal reflux disease, erosive esophagitis, ulcer symptoms, and gastroprotection in patients receiving non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, antiplatelet agents, or anticoagulants [ 14 ]. Therefore, reporting signals for proton pump inhibitors may reflect confounding by indication or protopathic bias rather than direct esophageal toxicity.

Statistical software and ethical considerations Primary data management was performed using PostgreSQL version 14.4, and the submitted primary analyses used R version 4.4.2. Reproducibility, sensitivity, and stratified analyses used R version 4.5.0, glmnet version 4.1–10, and openEBGM version 0.9.1. All statistical tests were two-sided where applicable. Bonferroni-adjusted P values < 0.01 were used for candidate screening; age-stratum heterogeneity P values were adjusted across 11 drug comparisons using the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) method.

This study used publicly available, anonymized, and de-identified spontaneous adverse event reporting data. No individual patient identifiers were accessed. Therefore, institutional review board approval and informed consent were not required.

Results Characteristics of FAERS reports A total of 8,061 FAERS reports met the prespecified composite case definition after deduplication and data cleaning (Fig. 1 A). Among these reports, 3,799 (47.1%) involved female patients and 3,529 (43.8%) involved male patients, while sex was missing or unknown in 733 reports (9.1%). Age was available in 6,013 reports and missing in 2,048 reports (25.4%). The largest age group was 18-64.9 years, accounting for 3,076 reports (38.2%), followed by 65–85 years with 2,453 reports (30.4%). Reports involving patients younger than 18 years and older than 85 years accounted for 215 (2.7%) and 269 (3.3%) reports, respectively. Body weight was missing in 5,534 reports (68.7%) (Table 1 ).

Serious outcomes were common. Hospitalization was reported in 3,831 reports (47.5%), death in 857 reports (10.6%), life-threatening events in 551 reports (6.8%), disability in 44 reports (0.5%), and required intervention in 21 reports (0.3%) (Fig. 1 D). These findings indicate that esophageal ulceration and perforation-related reports in FAERS frequently involved clinically serious outcomes.

Reporting frequency alone did not necessarily indicate a positive disproportionality signal. For example, adalimumab had a relatively high number of reports but did not show a positive ROR signal in FAERS. Therefore, frequency-based ranking was interpreted together with disproportionality analyses.

Disproportionality signals in FAERS Among the 50 most frequently reported FAERS primary-suspect drugs, the largest disproportionalityestimates were observed for doxycycline, alendronic acid, and clindamycin (Fig. 2 ). Doxycycline had an ROR of 41.15 (95% confidence interval [CI] 36.47–46.43), PRR of 40.48, EBGM of 38.59, and IC of 5.29. The corresponding estimates were ROR 21.45 (95% CI 19.14–24.04), PRR 21.27, EBGM 20.35, and IC 4.36 for alendronic acid; ROR 18.59 (95% CI 15.40-22.44), PRR 18.45, EBGM 17.89, and IC 4.19 for clindamycin; and ROR 10.82 (95% CI 9.66–12.13), PRR 10.78, EBGM 10.36, and IC 3.38 for esomeprazole. These values quantify reporting imbalance within FAERS and do not rank clinical risk.

Additional FAERS reporting signals were observed for antithrombotic and anti-inflammatory agents, including clopidogrel, acetylsalicylic acid, ibuprofen, dabigatran, rivaroxaban, warfarin, and naproxen. Signals were also observed for mycophenolic acid, tacrolimus, bevacizumab, and sunitinib. Across all 809 comparisons, 495 P values were obtained with Fisher’s exact test and 314 with Pearson’s chi-square test; 53 comparisons met the MGPS criterion of EBGM05 > 2. Complete drug-level results and multiplicity-adjusted P values are provided in Supplementary Table S2 .

The volcano plot displays reporting imbalance against Bonferroni-adjusted statistical prominence (Fig. 2 C). PPI-related points were interpreted cautiously because treatment indication and prodromal symptoms may influence reporting.

Large disproportionality estimates were observed for doxycycline hyclate, crizotinib, dabigatran etexilate methanesulfonate, alendronate sodium hydrate, minodronic acid hydrate, and sodium risedronate. These estimates were calculated within JADER and were not compared numerically with FAERS or Canada Vigilance.

Immune checkpoint inhibitor reports were present in JADER, but the prespecified positive-signal criteria were not met for nivolumab, pembrolizumab, or ipilimumab. JADER therefore showed descriptive overlap for several classic irritants, dabigatran, bisphosphonates, antiplatelet agents, and selected oncology therapies, without providing formal external validation.

Several biologic or immunomodulating product entries were frequently reported in Canada Vigilance, but not all met the signal criteria. IPILIMUMAB and NIVOLUMAB estimates were based on six and five composite-outcome reports, respectively, and were interpreted as exploratory. The RABEPRAZOLE signal was susceptible to confounding by indication and protopathic bias. Brand, biosimilar, and generic rows were retained separately and were not summed. These findings show descriptive overlap and heterogeneity, not confirmation of FAERS associations.

At lambda.min = 1.128109 × 10 -5 , all 11 had nonzero coefficients and were included in the multivariable logistic regression with age and sex (Fig. 5 A and B). The same variables remained nonzero at lambda.1se. The absence of variable reduction limits the incremental selection value of LASSO in this prescreened set.

In the valid-age FAERS case/non-case model, all 11 drug variables had adjusted odds ratios above 1 (Fig. 5 D). The largest adjusted odds ratios (ORs) were observed for doxycycline (25.98, 95% confidence interval [CI] 20.27–33.29), alendronic acid (25.38, 95% CI 20.60-31.27), clindamycin (11.03, 95% CI 7.16–16.99), and esomeprazole (10.16, 95% CI 8.38–12.32). These estimates describe adjusted reporting associations within the restricted regression sample and are not clinical risk estimates.

Age had a statistically detectable but small adjusted odds ratio (OR 1.011 per year, 95% CI 1.009–1.013). Neither female sex (OR 0.73, 95% CI 0.46–1.16) nor male sex (OR 0.99, 95% CI 0.62–1.58) showed a clear association relative to missing, unknown, or other sex. The apparent area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was 0.677 in the same sample (Fig. 5 C), indicating limited discrimination. Because no internal or external validation was performed, the model should not be used for individual prediction or clinical decision-making.

The distribution was heterogeneous, with both a concentration of short recorded intervals and a substantial long right tail (Fig. 6 A and B). The long intervals may reflect long-term treatment, delayed recognition or reporting, inaccurate therapy dates, treatment interruption or re-exposure, disease progression, or concomitant treatment. The data do not distinguish among these explanations.

Thirty-six drugs had upper 95% confidence limits for the shape parameter below 1 and were classified statistically as early-failure patterns; metformin had a confidence interval including 1 and was classified as random failure. These classifications describe fitted recorded-onset distributions and do not establish a clinical early-onset period.
