Sensitivity analysis excluding PPI-containing reports Within the restricted preprocessing object, 419,314 PPI-containing reports, including 662 composite-outcome reports, were excluded. The remaining sample comprised 2,700,725 reports, including 1,475 composite-outcome reports. Across the 10 non-PPI candidates, ROR changes ranged from − 9.2% to + 27.6%. Post-exclusion RORs were 25.01 (95% CI 19.08–32.80) for doxycycline, 23.15 (95% CI 18.30-29.28) for alendronic acid, and 10.76 (95% CI 6.84–16.94) for clindamycin. No algorithm-specific signal classification changed (Supplementary Table S3 ).

Age-stratified reporting patterns The age-stratified analysis included 3,119,650 reports with valid ages, including 2,136 composite-outcome reports. The < 65-year group contained 1,965,030 reports, including 1,152 composite-outcome reports; the ≥65-year group contained 1,154,620 reports, including 984 composite-outcome reports. Doxycycline had an ROR of 30.37 (95% CI 23.32–39.55) in the younger group and 5.25 (95% CI 2.49–11.06) in the older group, giving an older-to-younger ROR ratio of 0.173 (95% CI 0.078–0.381; BH-adjusted P = 0.000149). Esomeprazole also showed lower disproportionality in the older group (ROR ratio 0.535, 95% CI 0.357–0.802; BH-adjusted P = 0.0135). No other candidate met the multiplicity-adjusted heterogeneity criterion. Mycophenolic acid had no composite-outcome reports in the older stratum, so its continuity-corrected estimate was imprecise (Supplementary Table S4 ).

Integrated signal pattern Taken together, FAERS showed prominent reporting signals for established esophageal irritants, particularly doxycycline, alendronic acid, and clindamycin, alongside exploratory patterns for NSAIDs, antithrombotic agents, and immunosuppressants. JADER and Canada Vigilance showed overlapping but heterogeneous database-specific patterns. The regression analysis provided limited exploratory prioritization, and the onset analyses showed temporal heterogeneity rather than a single clinical risk window.

Discussion Principal findings and study contribution The principal finding was that the largest FAERS disproportionality estimates among common primary suspects involved established pill-injury drugs, particularly doxycycline, alendronic acid, and clindamycin. Descriptive overlap for selected drug-event pairs was observed in JADER and Canada Vigilance, but these database-specific estimates are not directly comparable and do not constitute external validation. The findings may help prioritize clinical awareness and further study, but they do not establish a hierarchy of drug-specific clinical risk.

The study also organized reports into clinically relevant contexts: classic local irritants, antithrombotic and NSAID therapies, immunosuppressive agents, and oncology-related therapies. These categories differ in biological plausibility, preventability, treatment context, and susceptibility to reporting bias. This framework aids interpretation but does not establish a common mechanism or causal contribution for every reported drug.

The findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating safety signals rather than causal risk estimates. Spontaneous reporting systems are valuable for detecting rare, serious, or unexpected adverse-event patterns after marketing, but they lack reliable exposure denominators and are affected by underreporting, duplicate reporting, stimulated reporting, incomplete clinical details, and confounding by indication [ 22 , 27 – 29 ]. Therefore, disproportionality measures and adjusted odds ratios from the restricted FAERS case/non-case model cannot be interpreted as incidence rates, absolute or comparative risks, or causal effect sizes. Their appropriate role is to support clinical signal recognition and prioritize drug-event pairs for further denominator-based pharmacoepidemiologic evaluation.

Classic pill-induced injury remains the most clinically actionable signal Doxycycline had one of the largest FAERS disproportionality estimates, consistent with established literature on pill-induced esophagitis [ 6 , 7 , 34 ]. Prolonged mucosal contact is plausible when a tablet or capsule is taken with insufficient water, before recumbency, or in the presence of dysphagia or impaired transit. Clinical reports continue to document doxycycline-associated esophageal ulceration [ 5 , 8 , 9 ]. This prior evidence supports biological plausibility, but the present ROR remains a measure of reporting imbalance rather than a causal effect size.

Alendronate-associated esophagitis and ulceration are well described, and administration precautions are integral to prescribing [ 4 , 35 , 36 ]. The FAERS pattern and descriptive overlap in JADER indicate continued post-marketing reporting despite long-standing awareness. They support reinforcing existing administration advice, not estimating additional incidence or comparative risk.

Clindamycin-induced esophageal injury may be difficult to recognize because its symptoms can resemble reflux disease, infection, or nonspecific retrosternal discomfort [ 10 , 37 , 38 ]. Its prominent FAERS signal supports continued clinical awareness [ 10 , 39 ]. Doxycycline, alendronic acid, and clindamycin therefore form a plausible group for administration counseling, while the current data remain insufficient for causal ranking.

Antithrombotic and NSAID-related signals broaden the clinical spectrum Reporting signals involving acetylsalicylic acid, clopidogrel, dabigatran, rivaroxaban, ibuprofen, and related agents broadened the observed context beyond classic local irritation [ 15 , 16 ]. These patterns should not be interpreted as proof of direct esophageal toxicity. They may reflect bleeding from an existing lesion, impaired recovery, older age, cardiovascular morbidity, polypharmacy, treatment indication, or differential surveillance.

Dabigatran warrants clinical attention because prior endoscopic evidence describes a recognizable esophageal injury pattern [ 11 , 12 ]. Its tartaric acid-containing capsule may contribute to local irritation [ 11 , 12 ]. The FAERS and JADER findings are consistent with that prior concern, but recurrence across spontaneous reporting systems remains descriptive and does not quantify individual risk.

For NSAIDs and antiplatelet agents, interpretation should remain cautious. These drugs may contribute to mucosal vulnerability or bleeding once injury occurs, but the observed reporting signals may also reflect age, cardiovascular comorbidity, concomitant medications, gastroprotective prescribing, and greater clinical surveillance. Therefore, these signals should be interpreted as prompts for medication review and clinical evaluation rather than as evidence of direct esophageal toxicity [ 14 ].

Immunosuppressive and oncology-related signals require context-specific interpretation The reporting spectrum also included immunosuppressive and oncology-related therapies, including mycophenolic acid, tacrolimus, bevacizumab, sunitinib, fluorouracil, cisplatin, crizotinib, and selected immune checkpoint inhibitors [ 17 , 40 – 43 ]. These estimates are especially vulnerable to treatment-context bias because recipients may have malignancy, transplantation, opportunistic infection, prior radiotherapy, procedural exposure, or extensive polypharmacy [ 18 , 20 ].

Mycophenolate-related gastrointestinal mucosal injury has been described in previous pathological studies [ 19 ]. In immunocompromised patients, ulcerative esophageal disease may also arise from opportunistic infections such as cytomegalovirus or herpes simplex virus [ 17 , 18 , 20 ]. Therefore, signals involving immunosuppressants may reflect direct mucosal injury, impaired epithelial repair, infection susceptibility, underlying disease severity, or concomitant therapy. The present data cannot distinguish among these possibilities. Accordingly, these signals should be interpreted as context-dependent reporting associations rather than evidence of a specific causal pathway.

Immune checkpoint inhibitor-related reports require particular caution. Although immune-mediated esophagitis has been described [ 21 , 44 , 45 ], positive signals in this study were confined mainly to small-count Canada Vigilance observations and were not reproduced as positive signals for nivolumab, pembrolizumab, or ipilimumab in JADER. These database-specific patterns warrant clinical review rather than causal attribution.

Potential confounding and reporting biases across drug categories Interpretation depends on why a drug was prescribed and the clinical setting in which a report arose. Confounding by indication is plausible when the treated condition itself predisposes to esophageal injury; protopathic bias may occur when a drug is prescribed for early symptoms of an unrecognized event; and channeling bias may arise when patients with greater baseline susceptibility receive a particular therapy. PPI signals are especially susceptible because these agents are prescribed for reflux, erosive esophagitis, ulcer symptoms, and gastroprotection [ 24 ].

Established pill irritants have stronger prior biological and clinical support, but their signal magnitudes may still be influenced by dysphagia, impaired mobility, administration technique, older age, and stimulated reporting. Antithrombotic and NSAID patterns may reflect cardiovascular and gastrointestinal comorbidity, bleeding from an existing lesion, or delayed healing rather than initiation of mucosal injury. Age- and sex-adjustment cannot resolve these factors.

For immunosuppressive and antineoplastic therapies, confounding by indication and channeling bias are particularly plausible because treated populations may have malignancy, transplantation, infection susceptibility, prior radiotherapy, mucosal injury from other treatments, invasive procedures, polypharmacy, or intensive surveillance. The available data cannot separate these explanations from possible drug-related contributions.

The PPI-exclusion analysis produced no change in algorithm-specific classifications for the 10 non-PPI candidates within the restricted sample. This finding does not remove confounding by indication, protopathic bias, unrecorded concomitant therapy, or selection introduced by preprocessing.

Age-stratified reporting patterns Lower relative reporting was observed for doxycycline and esomeprazole in reports involving adults aged 65 years or older; the remaining candidates did not show multiplicity-adjusted heterogeneity. Differences may reflect prescribing, formulation, medication burden, dysphagia, esophageal motility, comorbidity, missingness, or reporting behavior rather than biological effect modification. The restricted sample and absence of age-specific exposure denominators preclude inference about incidence or causal risk.

Temporal pattern and clinical implications The time-to-onset analysis describes intervals recorded for drug-report pairs, not event incidence over time. The nearly equal proportions of records at 0–30 days and beyond 360 days demonstrate substantial heterogeneity. Inaccurate or incomplete therapy dates, delayed recognition or reporting, long-term treatment, interruption or re-exposure, disease progression, and concomitant treatment may all contribute [ 46 , 47 ].

A Weibull shape estimate below 1 describes a decreasing pattern within the fitted recorded-onset distribution but does not define a clinical early-onset period or biological risk window. The absence of exposure-based risk sets, censoring, verified timelines, and independence among drug-report records precludes hazard interpretation. The scale and shape parameters are therefore descriptive summaries only [ 33 ].

The practical implication is focused clinical awareness rather than automatic treatment change. Administration counseling is appropriate for established pill-injury drugs. New odynophagia, dysphagia, retrosternal pain, hematemesis, or unexplained upper gastrointestinal symptoms after treatment initiation should prompt clinical assessment. For antithrombotic, NSAID, immunosuppressive, and oncology therapies, evaluation should include co-medications and alternative causes such as infection, malignancy-related injury, radiotherapy, or pre-existing esophageal disease.

Strengths and limitations This study focused on clinically important esophageal ulceration- and perforation-related events and analyzed three reporting systems separately. The use of four disproportionality algorithms, reproducible exploratory regression, descriptive onset analyses, and explicit bias assessment provides several complementary views of the reporting data. The multidatabase design permits descriptive comparison of overlap and heterogeneity, not formal external validation.

Several limitations must be acknowledged. Spontaneous reporting systems are subject to underreporting, duplicate and stimulated reporting, missing information, variable report quality, and the absence of exposure denominators; incidence, comparative risk, and causal effects therefore cannot be estimated. Indication, comorbidities, dysphagia, pre-existing esophageal disease, formulation, administration technique, endoscopic findings, infection, malignancy, radiotherapy, and concomitant treatment were unavailable or incomplete. The regression adjusted only for age and sex and used a restricted preprocessing object selected by data completeness. Candidate indicators were based on one standardized primary-suspect DRUG value per report, all 11 prescreened drugs remained in the model, and the apparent AUC of 0.677 indicated limited discrimination and was not internally or externally validated. The PPI-exclusion and age-stratified analyses used the same restricted object and may therefore be affected by selection.

Time-to-onset records were available only for selected drug-report pairs with valid dates, were not necessarily independent, and may contain date error or reporting delay. Canada Vigilance rows were product-name-specific and could not be combined reliably without report-level identifiers. The eight preferred terms pooled ulceration, hemorrhage, rupture, and perforation despite differences in severity, mechanism, and drug attribution; the preferred-term sex analysis did not provide drug-specific outcome or severity stratification. Accordingly, the present analysis cannot determine whether established local irritants and antithrombotic agents differ in their component-specific reporting patterns. Clinically adjudicated, outcome- and severity-stratified denominator-based studies are therefore needed. E-values were not calculated because spontaneous-reporting RORs measure reporting imbalance rather than causal risk and do not provide the causal estimand, exposure denominators, sampling probabilities, or confounder measurement required for interpretable E-value analysis.

Overall, the data identify prominent reporting patterns for established pill-injury drugs and exploratory patterns in other treatment contexts. Their appropriate use is to support clinical awareness and prioritize denominator-based pharmacoepidemiologic validation, not to infer causal rank or comparative drug risk.

Conclusion This multidatabase pharmacovigilance analysis identified disproportionate reporting patterns for selected drug-event pairs involving esophageal ulceration- and perforation-related events. The largest FAERS estimates among common primary suspects involved doxycycline, alendronic acid, and clindamycin; other drug categories showed exploratory, context-dependent patterns. These findings are hypothesis-generating and should not be interpreted as estimates of incidence, comparative clinical risk, or causal effects. Further evaluation requires data sources with exposure denominators, validated outcomes, and adequate control of confounding.

The work cannot be changed in any way or used commercially without permission from the journal. Bisphosphonates (BPs; alendronate and risedronate) have been approved as a therapy for osteoporosis. While the efficacy of these drugs appears similar, differences in safety and gastrointestinal tract (GIT) adverse effects are lacking. Consequently, a systematic review and a meta-analysis were carried out reporting on the incidence rate of GIT adverse effects and the safety of alendronate versus risedronate. In this study, the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines were used. This study collected articles from Embase, PubMed, Cochrane library, and Web of Science. Only RCTs that focused on the comparison between alendronate and risedronate in treating patients with osteoporosis were included. Risk ratios (RRs), 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and random-effects model were calculated. This meta-analysis identified 2202 studies including 4151 participants. There were six eligible RCTs. The incidence rate of GIT adverse effects in patients who received alendronate was 20.19%, while the incidence rate in patients who received risedronate was 18.30%. The rate of GIT adverse effects was not significantly different with alendronate compared to risedronate (RR: 1.11; 95% CI: 0.86–1.42; P < 0.44). In this review, the incidence rate of alendronate-associated gastrointestinal (GI) adverse effects was slightly higher than the incidence rate of risedronate-associated GI adverse effects. Although the finding is not statistically significant, switching the patient from alendronate to risedronate may nevertheless lower the incidence rate of GI side effects.

Résumé Les bisphosphonates (alendronate et risédronate) sont approuvés pour le traitement de l’ostéoporose. Bien que leur efficacité semble similaire, les différences en matière de sécurité et d’effets indésirables gastro-intestinaux restent à déterminer. Par conséquent, une revue systématique et une méta-analyse ont été réalisées afin d’évaluer l’incidence des effetsindésirables GI et la sécurité de l’alendronate par rapport au risédronate. Cette étude a suivi les recommandations PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses). Les articles ont été collectés dansles bases de données Embase, PubMed, Cochrane Library et Web of Science. Seulsles essais contrôlésrandomisés (ECR) comparant l’alendronate et le risédronate dansle traitement de l’ostéoporose ont été inclus. Les risques relatifs (RR), les intervalles de confiance (IC) à 95 % et un modèle à effets aléatoires (EA) ont été calculés. Cette méta-analyse a identifié 2 202 études incluant 4 151 participants. Six ECR ont été retenus. L’incidence des effets indésirables gastro-intestinaux chez les patients traités par alendronate était de 20,19 %, contre 18,30 % chez ceux traités par risédronate. Cette différence n’était pas significative (RR: 1,11 ; IC à 95 % : 0,86 à 1,42 ; P < 0,44). Dans cette étude, l’incidence des effets indésirables gastro-intestinaux associés à l’alendronate était légèrement supérieure à celle associée au risédronate. Bien que non statistiquement significative, cette différence pourrait permettre de réduire l’incidence de ces effets indésirables en optant pour le risédronate.

Trials of some of these drugs have reported a decrease in vertebral fracture incidence.[ 16 17 ] BPs are considered primary drugs used to correct the imbalance in bone formation.[ 18 19 ] In Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs), BP use for the long term showed improvement of BMD and a decrease in the risk of fracture.[ 20 ] This study will focus on the BP group, particularly alendronate and risedronate. Alendronate (alendronic acid) is a nitrogen-containing BP, which inhibits bone resorption by osteoclasts by binding to bone surfaces.[ 21 22 ] Indeed, a decrease in bone turnover to normal premenopausal levels is one of the beneficial effects of alendronate.[ 23 ] Notably, there is evidence of an increase in bone mineral density of the spine, hip, and total body in women with osteoporosis when taking daily treatment with oral alendronate for 3 years.[ 24 25 ] In addition, there was an association with lowering the incidence of vertebral fractures, deformities, and loss of height.[ 26 27 ] Another study also demonstrated that there was a significant decrease in morphometric, clinical vertebral fractures, and other clinical fractures when women with low bone mass were taking alendronate.[ 28 29 ] Some studies stated that there was a 44% decrease in radiographic vertebral fracture when taking alendronate.[ 30 31 ] Risedronate, also known as risedronic acid, can inhibit bone absorption by the inhibition of osteoclasts.[ 32 ] Risedronate has been reported to decrease fractures in postmenopausal osteoporosis. Risedronate has also been used to treat Paget’s disease and prevents corticosteroid-induced bone loss.[ 33 34 ] Notably, risedronate has been reported to drastically increase bone mineral density in the spine and hip within 6 months of use.[ 35 36 ] Indeed, risedronate can decrease vertebral fractures by 49% and the nonvertebral fractures by 33% over 3 years.[ 37 38 ] Although risedronate and alendronate share similar mechanisms of action, they have several differences. For example, the increase in bone mineral density and decrease in turnover marker levels in patients on alendronate is more marked than those on risedronate.[ 39 ] This study highlights the incidence rate of gastrointestinal (GI) adverse effects between the alendronate and risedronate and the safety of those drugs.

M ETHODOLOGY Search strategy PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were searched to retrieve all relevant articles until October 2024. The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses reporting guidelines were used to collect all articles about alendronate and risedronate and their GI adverse effects [ Figure 1 ].[ 40 ] Then, the articles that matched with our inclusion and did not match with the exclusion criteria were included in this systematic review and meta-analysis. Searching using the search terms “Alendronate,” “Risedronate,” and “Gastrointestinal Manifestations.” Literature retrieval was restricted to English only, and no restriction was performed on the publication date. Communication with the original authors was done in case of any unclear reported data.
Figure 1 Flow diagram of the study selection process (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses)

Selection criteria A through literature search was done for studies that compared alendronate versus risedronate on the incidence rate of GI tract (GIT) adverse events. Inclusion criteria were done based on the PICOS (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, Study design) method.[ 41 ] We included only original studies published in English and reporting on GIT adverse effect related to the use of alendronate or risedronate. In this study, the evaluation indicators were GIT adverse events incidence rate related to alendronate and risedronate and the risk ratio (RR). Population: any patients diagnosed with osteoporosis and using alendronate or risedronate for treatment. Intervention/comparison: Alendronate/risedronate. Outcomes: incidence rate of alendronate GIT adverse event compared to risedronate. Study design: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The exclusion criteria of the study were as follows: non-English studies. Duplicate studies: Case reports and review articles.

Data extraction Eligible studies were assessed, and the following information was gathered: author name, year of publication, study location, study design, study title, patient count, and course duration. The data extraction process was carried out independently by two reviewers (H. Karrar and Y. Nouh). Any disagreements were addressed by a third reviewer (R. Alhendi).

Data analysis and risk of bias Mantel–Haenszel RRs along with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using random-effects models. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The quality of each individual study was evaluated using the Cochrane Collaboration’s tool for assessing risk of bias.[ 42 ] All these analyses were carried out using Review Manager (RevMan is a program developed by Cochrane Collaboration Company, registered in England and Wales). RevMan is a tool developed by the Cochrane Library for creating and maintaining reviews that encompass language, research characteristics, comparison tables, and study data. It is capable of performing a meta-analysis on the provided data and visually presenting the results.

R ESULTS Results of literature search A total of 2202 studies were initially identified. A total of 2196 studies were excluded after a screening of titles and abstracts. After thorough review of the remaining articles, the authors decided to include six studies in this systematic review and meta-analysis.[ 39 44 45 46 47 48 ] These studies including 4151 patients who met the inclusion criteria for systematic review and meta-analysis. The selection process is shown in Figure 2 . Figure 2 Quality assessment of the included studies

Study characteristics The characteristics of the six included studies are summarized in Table 1 . The studies were conducted on more than 78 continents. The mean or median patient age ranged from 53 to 72 years. Four studies focused patients who are women with osteoporosis[ 39 43 44 47 ] and two studies included any hospitalized patient with osteoporosis.[ 44 46 48 ] The duration of drug therapy ranged from 14 days to 24 months. The alendronate dose used was 10 mg/day[ 45 47 ] or 70 mg/week,[ 39 43 44 46 48 ] and the risedronate dose was 5 mg/day[ 44 45 47 ] or 35 mg/week.[ 39 45 46 48 ] Table 2 shows the characteristics of patients. The mean age of the included patients was 63.36 years.[ 39 44 45 46 47 48 ] The mean age since menopause was 18.5 years.[ 39 43 44 46 48 ] 90.7% of the patients were Caucasian.[ 39 43 44 47 ] Two studies included patients who consumed alcohol,[ 45 47 ] and two studies included patients who were smokers.[ 45 47 ]

Study outcome The incidence rate of GIT adverse effects in patients who received alendronate was 20.19%, while the incidence rate in patients who received risedronate was 18.30%. The rate of GIT adverse effects was not significantly different with alendronate than with risedronate (RR: 1.11; 95% CI: 0.86–1.42; P < 0.44) as shown in Figure 3 . D ISCUSSION Adverse effects may be gastric or duodenal perforations, ulcers, and bleeding. This meta-analysis of RCTs confirms a little different in rate of GIT adverse effects, occurring in approximately one-fifth of patients treated with alendronate or risedronate regimens. However, individual studies have described incidences ranging from 15% up to 30%. This variability is due to diversity of patient populations, ranges of doses used, duration of the treatments, the differences in severity of the illness, and the presence of potential confounders such as concomitant use of other agents that may cause GIT adverse effects. In addition, we analyzed only studies that were randomized controlled studies. There are several risk factors including advanced age, presence of chronic comorbid conditions, gender, diet, and estrogen level which contributed to risedronate and alendronate-induced GI adverse effects.[ 6 9 ] In this study, the mean/median age of patients in most included studies was above 60 years of age, and the average baseline years since menopause was around 20 years. Other patient-specific data were not uniformly reported in the included studies. The risk for GIT adverse effects may also be associated with the duration of risedronate or alendronate therapy. There are several strengths to this analysis. We included only randomized controlled studies. All studies included were double-blinded. In addition, the population was representative of patients from more than 78 continents, and the sample size for each study was large. Several limitations related to this study are worthy of consideration. The RCTs used variable doses for alendronate and risedronate, which can make clinical application challenging. There is a possibility that alendronate or risedronate-associated GIT adverse effects incidence was inflated due to patients’ ages as all were above 60 years of age, consumption of alcohol, and consumption of tobacco. The overall sample size in this analysis was relatively small, and no significant differences were found between the two groups in the percentage of patients who received alendronate and risedronate. Direct comparison between alendronate and risedronate needs further studies to identify. Finally, there was insufficient detail to examine the progression and resolution of GIT adverse effects along a continuum among the individual studies.

C ONCLUSION In this meta-analysis, the incidence rate of alendronate-associated GI adverse effects was found to be slightly higher than the incidence rate of risedronate-associated GI adverse effects. Although the finding is not statistically significant, switching the patient from alendronate to risedronate may nevertheless lower the incidence rate of GI side effects. Esophagitis dissecans superficialis (EDS), also referred to as “sloughing esophagitis,” is an uncommon benign condition characterized by the desquamation of the superficial layer of the esophageal squamous mucosa. It is often underdiagnosed due to its rarity and nonspecific clinical presentation. Although several factors such as caustic ingestion, thermal injury, autoimmune disorders, and mechanical trauma have been implicated, medication-induced mucosal injury remains one of the most significant causes. Among these, bisphosphonates – a class of drugs widely prescribed for osteoporosis and other bone-related disorders – have been identified as a potential offending agent. We report the case of a 66-year-old woman with no significant comorbidities who presented with persistent retrosternal burning and pain for 2 months. There was no associated dysphagia, odynophagia, vomiting, hematemesis, weight loss, or history of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use. Physical and systemic examinations were unremarkable. Despite treatment with double-dose esomeprazole for 8 weeks, her symptoms persisted. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed a large area of whitish sloughed-off mucosa overlying a superficial ulcer with regular margins, extending from 26 cm to just above the gastroesophageal junction. A detailed drug history subsequently revealed the use of bisphosphonate gel for osteoporosis. Histopathological analysis demonstrated sloughed squamous epithelium with the features of superficial mucosal necrosis, confirming the diagnosis of EDS secondary to bisphosphonate-induced chemical injury. Discontinuation of the bisphosphonate and continuation of proton-pump inhibitor therapy led to complete symptom resolution within 2 weeks. This case underscores the importance of considering drug-induced esophageal injury in patients with refractory retrosternal pain unresponsive to acid suppression therapy. Bisphosphonates, although highly effective in osteoporosis management, may cause significant mucosal damage when not used properly. Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion for bisphosphonate-induced EDS, as timely recognition and withdrawal of the offending agent usually result in rapid clinical and endoscopic improvement.

Résumé L’œsophagite disséquante superficielle (EDS), également appelée « œsophagite desquamative », est une affection bénigne rare caractérisée par la desquamation de la couche superficielle de la muqueuse squameuse de l’œsophage. Elle est souvent sous-diagnostiquée en raison de sa rareté et de sa présentation clinique non spécifique. Bien que plusieurs facteurs tels que l’ingestion de substances caustiques, les lésions thermiques, les maladies auto-immunes et les traumatismes mécaniques aient été impliqués, les lésions muqueuses induites par des médicaments restent l’une des causes les plus importantes. Parmi celles-ci, les bisphosphonates – une classe de médicaments largement prescrits pour l’ostéoporose et d’autres troubles osseux – ont été identifiés comme un agent potentiellement responsable. Nous rapportons le cas d’une femme de 66 ans, sans comorbidités significatives, qui s’est présentée avec des brûlures et des douleurs rétrosternales persistantes depuis 2 mois. Il n’y avait pas de dysphagie, d’odynophagie, de vomissements, d’hématémèse, de perte de poids ni d’antécédents de prise d’anti-inflammatoires non stéroïdiens. L’examen clinique et systémique était sans particularités. Malgré un traitement par ésoméprazole à double dose pendant 8 semaines, les symptômes ont persisté. L’endoscopie digestive haute a révélé une large zone de muqueuse blanchâtre desquamée recouvrant un ulcère superficiel aux marges régulières, s’étendant de 26 cm jusqu’au-dessus de la jonction gastro-œsophagienne. Une anamnèse médicamenteuse détaillée a ensuite mis en évidence l’utilisation d’un gel de bisphosphonate pour l’ostéoporose. L’analyse histopathologique a montré un épithélium squameux desquamé avec des caractéristiques de nécrose muqueuse superficielle, confirmant le diagnostic d’EDS secondaire à une lésion chimique induite par les bisphosphonates. L’arrêt du bisphosphonate et la poursuite du traitement par inhibiteur de la pompe à protons ont conduit à une résolution complète des symptômes en 2 semaines. Ce cas souligne l’importance de considérer une atteinte œsophagienne induite par les médicaments chez les patients présentant des douleurs rétrosternales réfractaires au traitement antiacide. Les bisphosphonates, bien qu’efficaces dans la prise en charge de l’ostéoporose, peuvent provoquer des lésions muqueuses significatives lorsqu’ils ne sont pas utilisés correctement. Les cliniciens doivent maintenir un haut niveau de suspicion pour une EDS induite par les bisphosphonates, car une reconnaissance précoce et l’arrêt de l’agent causal entraînent généralement une amélioration clinique et endoscopique rapide.

Although first described decades ago, it remains an under-recognized entity, largely due to its infrequent occurrence and nonspecific presentation. The true incidence of EDS is not well established; however, studies suggest it accounts for <0.03% of all upper gastrointestinal (UGI) endoscopies.[ 1 2 ]

Clinically, EDS can present with a wide range of manifestations – from being completely asymptomatic to causing symptoms such as retrosternal discomfort, odynophagia, dysphagia, or upper abdominal pain. In some cases, patients may even vomit whitish mucosal casts that resemble esophageal tissue. The nonspecific nature of these symptoms often leads to misdiagnosis or delayed diagnosis, especially in cases where more common conditions like gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) or peptic ulcer disease are suspected.[ 3 4 ]

The etiology of EDS is multifactorial. It may occur idiopathically or as a result of chemical, thermal, or mechanical mucosal injury. Commonly implicated agents include medications such as bisphosphonates, potassium chloride, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), iron supplements, and psychoactive drugs. Other associated factors include caustic ingestion, autoimmune blistering diseases (such as pemphigus vulgaris), celiac disease, and prolonged mucosal irritation due to reflux or infections.[ 5 6 ]

Bisphosphonates, in particular, are well-documented to cause esophageal irritation and ulceration due to their caustic properties. These drugs, often prescribed for osteoporosis and metastatic bone disease, can cause localized mucosal injury when they come into prolonged contact with the esophageal lining, especially if not swallowed with adequate water or when used in topical or gel formulations. The pathophysiology involves direct chemical injury leading to necrosis of the superficial epithelial layer, resulting in sloughing and ulcer formation.[ 7 8 ]

Endoscopically, EDS is characterized by the presence of long, whitish, or grayish sloughed mucosal sheets lining the esophagus, often overlying a hyperemic or ulcerated mucosa. Histologically, it shows separation of the superficial epithelium from the underlying viable mucosa, without significant inflammatory infiltration or dysplasia.

Given its self-limiting nature, EDS often resolves spontaneously once the offending agent is discontinued. However, its recognition is important to prevent unnecessary invasive procedures or prolonged use of inappropriate medications. Here, we present a case of bisphosphonate-induced EDS in an elderly woman who presented with persistent retrosternal pain, emphasizing the need for careful drug history and awareness of this rare but significant adverse drug effect.

C ASE R EPORT A 66-year-old postmenopausal woman presented to the outpatient department with complaints of retrosternal burning sensation and intermittent dull pain in the central chest region for the past 2 months. The pain was described as nonradiating, moderate in intensity, and not related to meals or posture. There was no history of dysphagia, odynophagia, vomiting, hematemesis, regurgitation, or heartburn prior to this episode. She denied any history of weight loss, anorexia, or melena. The patient had no known history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, ischemic heart disease, or chronic liver or kidney disease.

She reported no history of chronic medication use, alcohol intake, or tobacco consumption. There was no history suggestive of reflux symptoms or any prior gastrointestinal disorder. Importantly, she denied taking any NSAIDs, corticosteroids, or potassium supplements. There was no history of caustic ingestion or radiation exposure. On general physical examination, she was afebrile, with stable vital parameters. Her nutritional status was adequate, and no signs of anemia, dehydration, or systemic illness were present. Systemic examination of the cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal systems was unremarkable.

A clinical diagnosis of refractory GERD or nonulcer dyspepsia was initially considered. She was started on a double-dose proton-pump inhibitor (esomeprazole 40 mg twice daily) for 8 weeks, along with dietary modifications and lifestyle advice. Despite strict adherence to the prescribed regimen, the patient reported no significant improvement in her symptoms.

Due to persistence of pain, she was referred for an UGI endoscopy. Endoscopic evaluation revealed a striking finding [ Figure 1 ] – a large segment of whitish, thick sloughed-off mucosal sheets extending longitudinally along the lower esophagus, with an underlying superficial ulceration exhibiting regular margins and a smooth base. The lesion began approximately 26 cm from the upper incisors and extended distally up to just above the gastroesophageal (GE) junction. There was mild surrounding mucosal erythema but no evidence of nodularity, strictures, or mass lesions. The stomach and duodenal mucosa appeared normal. The endoscopic appearance was suggestive of sloughing esophagitis or EDS.

Figure 1 Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy Biopsy specimens were obtained from the affected region, including both the sloughed mucosa and the ulcer base, for histopathological examination. Meanwhile, a detailed review of the patient’s medical history was undertaken to identify the possible etiological factors. On careful re-evaluation, the patient revealed that she had been applying a topical bisphosphonate gel preparation on her gums and oral mucosa for the management of osteoporosis-related dental sensitivity over the past 3 months. She had not previously disclosed this detail, as she considered the gel a “local vitamin preparation” and not a medication relevant to her esophageal symptoms.

Histopathological examination [ Figure 2 ] of the biopsy revealed the fragments of necrotic squamous epithelium with surface sloughing, acantholysis, and separation of the superficial epithelial layer from the underlying mucosa. The lamina propria showed minimal inflammatory infiltrate without evidence of fungal elements, viral cytopathic changes, or malignancy. These features were consistent with EDS, likely secondary to chemical injury from bisphosphonate exposure.

Figure 2 Histopathology. The arrow revealed the the fragments of necrotic squamous epithelium with surface sloughing, acantholysis, and separation of the superficial epithelial layer from the underlying mucosa. The magnification value was low to intermediate that 40x to 100x Following the histopathological confirmation, the bisphosphonate gel was immediately discontinued. The patient was advised to continue once-daily esomeprazole (40 mg) and avoid any chemical or topical oral preparations. She was counseled about adequate hydration and proper medication administration techniques.

On follow-up after 2 weeks, the patient reported the complete resolution of retrosternal pain and burning. A repeat endoscopic examination was not deemed necessary given the complete symptomatic relief. The patient remained asymptomatic on subsequent monthly follow-ups for 3 months. This clinical course, characterized by a strong temporal association between bisphosphonate use and symptom onset, endoscopic evidence of sloughed mucosa, and complete recovery upon discontinuation, confirmed the diagnosis of bisphosphonate-induced EDS.

D ISCUSSION EDS, also known as “sloughing esophagitis,” is a rare, benign condition characterized by the desquamation of the superficial layer of the esophageal squamous epithelium. Although the condition is uncommon, with a reported prevalence of <0.03% in endoscopic series,[ 1 ] it is likely underdiagnosed due to its nonspecific presentation and spontaneous resolution in many patients. EDS is usually identified incidentally during UGI endoscopy performed for unrelated complaints.

The exact pathogenesis of EDS remains unclear; however, mucosal injury due to chemical or mechanical insult is thought to play a central role. Various drugs have been implicated, including bisphosphonates, potassium chloride, NSAIDs, iron supplements, and certain psychoactive medications such as sertraline and methotrexate.[ 2 3 ] Other causative factors include ingestion of caustic substances, hot beverages, thermal injury, and autoimmune conditions such as pemphigus vulgaris and bullous pemphigoid.

Bisphosphonates, particularly alendronate and risedronate, are well known to cause esophageal irritation and ulceration. Their mechanism of injury involves direct mucosal toxicity due to the compound’s acidic pH and chelating properties. Bisphosphonates can adhere to the esophageal mucosa and, upon dissolution, cause localized chemical burns and necrosis of epithelial cells.[ 4 5 ] The resulting epithelial sloughing corresponds histologically to the characteristic findings of EDS – detachment of the superficial squamous layer from the basal zone with minimal inflammatory response. The risk of esophageal injury is significantly increased with improper administration (e.g., inadequate water intake, lying down soon after ingestion, or, as in this case, topical contact with mucosa through a gel formulation).

Clinically, EDS presents with a broad spectrum of symptoms ranging from mild retrosternal discomfort and heartburn to odynophagia, dysphagia, or even vomiting of esophageal casts.[ 6 ] In many cases, however, patients remain asymptomatic. Because symptoms overlap with more common conditions such as GERD, esophageal candidiasis, or peptic ulcer disease, diagnosis is often delayed or missed.

Endoscopic appearance is diagnostic in most cases. The hallmark feature is sloughed, whitish, or grayish mucosal sheets, often described as “membranous” lesions that can be peeled off, leaving behind a smooth or mildly erythematous surface. In severe cases, the mucosa may appear ulcerated or friable. In this patient, endoscopy revealed an extensive segment of sloughed mucosa with underlying superficial ulceration extending up to the gastroesophageal junction, consistent with the classical description of EDS.

Histopathological examination confirms the diagnosis and distinguishes EDS from other forms of esophagitis. The typical features include detachment of the superficial squamous epithelium, acantholysis, necrosis, and minimal inflammatory infiltrate in the lamina propria.[ 7 ] In this case, biopsy demonstrated necrotic sloughed squamous cells with minimal inflammation, ruling out infectious, reflux, or neoplastic causes. Differential diagnosis The differential diagnosis of EDS includes the several other causes of esophageal mucosal injury:

Pill-induced esophagitis Commonly caused by tetracyclines, potassium chloride, or NSAIDs, pill esophagitis usually presents with discrete ulcers rather than diffuse mucosal sloughing. Infectious esophagitis Candida , cytomegalovirus, and herpes simplex virus infections produce characteristic endoscopic and histological findings, including pseudomembranes, viral inclusions, or fungal hyphae, none of which were present in this case. Corrosive or caustic ingestion Typically presents with circumferential deep ulceration and fibrosis, often associated with stricture formation.

Autoimmune bullous disorders Diseases such as pemphigus vulgaris and bullous pemphigoid can cause esophageal desquamation but are usually associated with cutaneous or oral lesions and positive immunofluorescence findings.[ 8 ] Management and prognosis The treatment of EDS primarily involves the identification and removal of the inciting factor. In drug-induced cases, discontinuation of the offending agent leads to rapid symptom resolution, as observed in this patient. Supportive management with proton pump inhibitors aids mucosal healing and provides symptomatic relief.[ 9 ] Corticosteroids or immunosuppressive agents are reserved for autoimmune-associated cases.

The prognosis of EDS is excellent. Most cases resolve completely without complications once the causative agent is withdrawn. Recurrence is rare unless re-exposure occurs. In our patient, cessation of bisphosphonate gel use led to the complete symptom relief within 2 weeks, confirming the causal association.

Review of literature Several reports in the literature have described bisphosphonate-induced esophageal injury, but cases presenting specifically as EDS are rare. Purdy and Appelman[ 10 ] first described the condition as a distinct endoscopic and histologic entity. Carmack et al .,[ 1 ] in their analysis of 21 cases, noted that approximately one-third was associated with medication use, with bisphosphonates being one of the most common culprits. A more recent review by Ebigbo et al .[ 11 ] reiterated that bisphosphonate-induced EDS tends to occur in elderly women using oral or topical preparations and typically resolves with drug discontinuation and acid suppression therapy.

Our case adds to this growing body of evidence, emphasizing that not only oral ingestion but even topical bisphosphonate preparations can lead to mucosal injury through inadvertent esophageal exposure. Awareness of such atypical presentations is crucial to prevent misdiagnosis and unnecessary invasive procedures.

C ONCLUSION This case highlights the importance of a detailed medication history in all patients presenting with refractory retrosternal pain or atypical endoscopic findings. Bisphosphonate-induced EDS, although uncommon, should be considered in the differential diagnosis of esophageal ulceration, particularly in elderly women on osteoporosis therapy. Early recognition and prompt discontinuation of the offending agent can lead to complete recovery and prevent recurrence.

Objective To systematically identify drug-induced esophageal ulcer and address existing knowledge gaps.

Methods We conducted a real-world study using the Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System database from Q1 2004 to Q4 2024. Disproportionality analyses were performed to evaluate drug-induced esophageal ulcer risk. Data for each drug were merged and screened using the RxNax platform to recalculate drug exposure, proportional reporting ratio, reporting odds ratio, and chi-squared values. High-risk drugs classified by anatomical therapeutic chemical classification system were cross-checked with Side Effect Resource, product labels, and published literature.

Results A total of 12,763 drug-induced esophageal ulcer cases were identified. Forty-nine high-risk drugs, spanning nine anatomical therapeutic chemical classification system classes, were detected, including antineoplastics and immunomodulators (Class L), systemic anti-infectives (Class J), and drugs affecting the musculoskeletal system (Class M). Aspirin, alendronic acid, and doxycycline were most frequently reported; doxycycline, clindamycin, and alendronic acid generated the strongest safety signals. Antineoplastics/immunomodulators (anatomical therapeutic chemical classification system L) had the highest cumulative proportional reporting ratio, primarily driven by tacrolimus, mycophenolic acid, and sunitinib. Notably, tacrolimus, sunitinib, meclofenamic acid, clopidogrel, and erlotinib were associated with esophageal ulcers but remain unlabeled for this risk.

Conclusions This study provides a comprehensive drug-induced esophageal ulcer risk profile, highlighting high-risk drugs beyond commonly recognized agents. These findings can inform safer prescribing practices, patient counseling, and targeted pharmacovigilance. However, drug-induced esophageal ulcer (DEU)—defined as damage and ulceration of the esophageal mucosa caused by medications—poses a serious health threat. Typical clinical manifestations include sudden onset of retrosternal pain, dysphagia, and hematemesis, while endoscopic examination often reveals mucosal erythema, erosions, and microscopically distributed esophageal ulcers. 1 , 2 The pathomechanism of DEU involves direct chemical irritation of the esophageal mucosa by drugs, localized physical retention, and indirect effects mediated by systemic pharmacological actions.

3 DEU is frequently misdiagnosed or diagnosed late because its symptoms closely resemble those of gastroesophageal reflux disease. 4 Misdiagnosis may lead to unnecessary anti-reflux therapy, increasing the burden on the healthcare system. In addition, DEU can result in severe complications, including transmural perforation, stricture formation, and occult hemorrhage. 5 , 6 Case reports of DEU caused by drugs such as tetracycline, clindamycin, and potassium chloride date back to 1979. 7 In recent years, attention has also turned to the occurrence of DEU in the adolescent population. 8

Despite this, awareness of DEU risk remains limited. Clinicians often overlook DEU as a potential cause of chest pain or odynophagia, and its diagnosis is frequently underestimated because most patients report self-limiting symptoms. 9

Existing studies on DEU have several limitations. Case reports are neither sufficiently representative nor do they provide quantitative risk indicators. 10 – 14 Small clinical studies are usually single-center, limiting control over confounding factors. 8 , 15 In vitro or animal experiments do not accurately reflect human esophageal dynamics and often involve high drug concentrations, which restricts their clinical relevance. Collectively, these limitations make the current evidence insufficient to guide practice effectively.

DEU is a serious adverse drug reaction (ADR) that, although easily overlooked, should not be underestimated. Nevertheless, studies investigating associated drug–risk signals remain insufficiently systematic. The present study is a real-world pharmacovigilance analysis of DEU based on the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database. It aimed to expand the spectrum of risk-associated drugs and identify potential high-risk medications that have been underemphasized in previous literature.

Data and methods Data sources This retrospective study was conducted using the FAERS database. FAERS is designed to support post-market surveillance of drugs and therapeutic biologics and contains information on ADRs and medication errors collected by the FDA. 16 – 19 Data are voluntarily submitted by healthcare professionals and consumers and include demographic characteristics, drug information, clinical outcomes, and other relevant details. We queried the FAERS database using the OpenVigil 2.1 pharmacovigilance analytics platform. OpenVigil 2.1 is a publicly available tool that imports raw FAERS data and enables data extraction, cleaning, mining, and analysis. 20 , 21

Definition of ADRs and drugs ADRs in the FAERS database were coded according to the Preferred Term (PT) in the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA, Version 26.1). The PT hierarchy at level 4, which is most commonly used, was applied in this study. We searched for “Oesophageal ulcer” (MedDRA code: 10030201) in the PT column to identify drugs associated with esophageal ulceration. All corresponding reports were then downloaded. For statistical analysis, the generic drug name was used as the unique identifier. Many FAERS reports use brand names; these were converted to generic names using the DrugBank database. If a drug name could not be retrieved in DrugBank ( https://go.drugbank.com/drugs ), the report was considered incorrect and removed manually.

Determine the relevant anatomical therapeutic chemical classification system (ATC) code for drugs Drugs that met the screening criteria were checked against the ATC code on the World Health Organization (WHO) ATC/DDD index website ( https://www.whocc.no/atc_ddd_index/ ). The ATC system, the official classification system of the WHO for medicines, consists of five hierarchical levels. The first level is a single letter representing the anatomical classification. The second level is a two-digit code for therapeutic classification. The third level is a single letter indicating pharmacological classification. The fourth level is a single letter for chemical classification, and the fifth level is a two-digit number specifying the compound. Individual drugs may have multiple ATC codes; for this study, the ATC code corresponding to the first indication in the drug specification was selected. In this study, drugs causing DEU were classified anatomically using the first level of the ATC code and pharmacologically using the third level. A sunrise diagram was then created based on the proportional reporting ratio (PRR) value of each drug.

Excavation signal evaluation To comprehensively evaluate the validity of risk signals for adverse events, we searched for “esophageal ulcer” on the Side Effect Resource (SIDER) website ( http://sideeffects.embl.de/ ) and reviewed records of drugs reported to cause DEU. Drug inserts were individually examined to determine whether DEU-related ADRs were documented. Additionally, PubMed and China Knowledge Network were searched for studies or reports of related adverse events. The results were analyzed to evaluate the mining signals for adverse events, and a summary table was created to present the findings. This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki (1975, revised 2024). No AI-generated content or AI-assisted data analysis tools were used in the conception, design, execution, or interpretation of this research. The reporting of this study conforms to Standards for QUality Improvement Reporting Excellence (SQUIRE) guidelines. 16 , 19 , 22

Ethics statement This study analyzed data from a publicly available and anonymized resource. The FAERS database is designed to support FDA-approved drug safety surveillance programs and is accessible for research purposes. Therefore, this study did not require Institutional Review Board approval, nor did it require obtaining informed consent from patients.

Statistical analysis Disproportionality analysis was used to generate hypotheses regarding possible associations between drugs and esophageal ulcer. This method calculates the ratio of observed to expected drug–ADR reports, with significant imbalance indicated when a prespecified threshold is exceeded. ROR and PRR are the two most commonly used measures in disproportionality analysis, valued for their simplicity and consistent results. The calculation formulas and criteria are listed in Table 1 . Higher ROR or PRR values indicate a stronger statistical association between the suspected drug and the ADR. ROR and PRR values were initially calculated using OpenVigil 2.1, and subsequent data processing and analysis were performed using Microsoft Excel 2019.

Discussion OpenVigil 2.1, as a publicly available pharmacovigilance tool, overcomes technical limitations by integrating standardized MedDRA term mapping, a multi-algorithm signal detection framework, and a built-in time-series analysis module. It allows direct import and analysis of raw ADR data from the FAERS database. 20 , 21 This systematic study not only confirms DEU risk associated with well-established medications but also identifies significant safety signals for drugs not commonly recognized for this adverse effect.

A total of 12,763 DEU-related adverse event reports were identified, and 49 suspected drugs were analyzed. These drugs were broadly distributed across nine major ATC classifications, including antitumor and immunomodulating agents (Class L), systemic anti-infectives (Class J), and musculoskeletal system drugs (Class M). The three most frequently reported drugs were aspirin (frequency = 263), alendronate (frequency = 244), and doxycycline (frequency = 200). The three drugs with the highest signal intensities were doxycycline (PRR = 35.096), aluminum thioglycollate (PRR = 23.007), and clindamycin (PRR = 15.516). These results are consistent with prior knowledge that certain drugs carry a high risk of DEU.

Although previous studies often focused on specific drug classes, our analysis systematically screened 20 years of data (2004–2024) across all drug classes. Beyond confirming established associations, a key contribution of this study is the identification of significant DEU signals for drugs not currently listed in standard adverse effect databases (e.g. SIDER) or in their prescribing information. Notably, strong disproportionate signals were observed for tacrolimus, mycophenolic acid, sunitinib, clopidogrel, and erlotinib. These findings highlight potential “blind spots” in official safety profiles, particularly for high-risk populations such as immunocompromised or oncology patients. Clinicians should exercise heightened vigilance and counsel patients on esophageal symptoms when prescribing these agents, even in the absence of prior warnings. For regulators and the pharmacovigilance community, these signals warrant further investigation and consideration for label updates.

Retrospective studies have shown that antibiotics and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are major causes of drug-induced esophagitis, consistent with our findings. 23 Literature also documents DEU associated with bisphosphonates; one study reported that 10.7% of patients taking oral bisphosphonates developed gastric or esophageal symptoms. 24 Furthermore, the combination of bisphosphonates with antithrombotic drugs or NSAIDs increases mucosal injury and symptom severity. 25 , 26 Disproportionality analysis of the FAERS database similarly identified esophageal ulceration as a major adverse event of bisphosphonates. 26

Therefore, antibiotics, NSAIDs, and bisphosphonates should be considered high-risk medications for DEU. Particular caution is warranted when bisphosphonates are co-administered with antithrombotic drugs/NSAIDs; the clinical necessity of such combinations should be critically evaluated, and patient guidance on proper medication use should be strengthened. Doxycycline, a high-frequency, high-risk drug, exhibited a signal intensity far exceeding that of the traditionally recognized high-risk drug alendronate (PRR =13.525), suggesting that previous literature may have underestimated the risk of some drugs in this class. Carlborg et al.

27 conducted a clinical and experimental study on tetracycline-induced DEU as early as 1983, in which 40 of 100 patients taking oral tetracycline developed sudden onset of intense retrosternal pain and dysphagia. All patients had significant peri-esophageal ulceration. History, barium meal, esophagoscopy, biopsy, and esophageal manometry revealed no other obvious etiology, and the localized corrosive effect of tetracycline was implicated. Experimental testing in the cat esophagus further confirmed the severe localized corrosive effect of tetracycline. Additional case reports have also documented DEU caused by doxycycline. 13 , 28 , 29 Early clinical studies and animal experiments have established the mechanism of localized corrosion for tetracyclines, and as a derivative, doxycycline warrants heightened vigilance.

In this study, antitumor and immunomodulating agents (Class L) ranked first in cumulative PRR values in the ATC Class I classification, involving 12 drugs (24.5%, 12/49). The top three drugs most likely to cause DEUs in this category were tacrolimus, mycophenolic acid, and sunitinib. Tacrolimus ranked first in both frequency and signal strength. This drug was not listed in the SIDER database, and its prescribing information mentions gastrointestinal ulceration and perforation, oral mucositis, and ulceration, but does not specify esophageal ulceration. The first case report of tacrolimus-induced acute esophageal necrosis in 2020 highlights the potential for immunosuppressants to cause this rare adverse reaction.

30 Therefore, tacrolimus-induced DEU should be considered a significant concern requiring clinical vigilance. Other high-signal immunomodulators, including fluorouracil and mesalazine, have also been reported in the literature. 31 , 32 Among antitumor drugs, sunitinib exhibited the highest signal intensity, and Jeanniard-Malet et al. 33 reported three cases of severe ulcerative esophagitis induced by sunitinib. A study comparing erlotinib plus gemcitabine versus gemcitabine alone in advanced pancreatic cancer found a higher frequency of ulcers in the combination therapy group. 34

Literature searches have also identified novel antitumor agents such as bevacizumab and cetuximab as associated with esophageal ulcers. 35 , 36 Real-world data from this study, combined with increasing literature reports, indicate that the DEU risk associated with antitumor and immunomodulatory agents has been previously under-recognized and should be a focus of clinical concern. High-risk antitumor agents in patients with peptic ulcer disease require careful assessment, and monitoring for DEUs should be intensified. These agents are particularly relevant in chronic, high-stakes conditions (e.g. organ transplantation, cardiovascular disease, oncology), where early recognition of DEU can prevent serious complications. Clinicians are encouraged to enhance monitoring and patient education to identify DEU risk promptly.

Notably, thioglycollate, prochlorperazine, olmesartan ester, and azathioprine are not documented as causing DEU in drug inserts, the SIDER database, or relevant literature. The strong signals identified in this study suggest these potential risks warrant further validation, though they may represent false-positive signals. Conversely, tacrolimus, sunitinib, mycophenolic acid, clopidogrel, and erlotinib do not list esophageal ulceration in their prescribing information, yet real-world data and literature evidence indicate a clear risk. These findings help compensate for delays in drug insert updates, alert clinicians to previously underappreciated DEU risks, and enrich the catalog of major suspected drugs associated with DEUs in clinical practice.

The study also found that proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), such as esomeprazole (PRR = 6.004) and omeprazole (PRR =3.467), ranked as high-risk medications, which contradicts the previous notion that PPIs reduce the risk of DEU. Possible explanations include: (a) PPI users often concurrently take other high-risk medications (e.g. NSAIDs or antiplatelet agents), and confounding factors may not be fully controlled; (b) long-term acid suppression may lead to bacterial overgrowth in the stomach, which can secondarily damage the esophagus; and (c) PPIs themselves may interfere with the esophageal mucosal barrier via unknown mechanisms. This finding highlights the need for clinicians to re-evaluate the dual role of PPIs in DEU and avoid blind co-administration.

The mechanisms underlying DEUs are diverse and vary across drug classes. Bisphosphonates (e.g. alendronate, ibandronate) can cause direct chemical irritation of the mucosa, primarily due to their high acidity and the tendency of tablets to remain in the esophagus. Endoscopic findings typically reveal erosions or ulcerations, exudative inflammation, and esophageal wall thickening. 37

Patients who do not follow proper administration instructions—taking the medication upright and with sufficient water—may experience prolonged drug adhesion to the esophageal wall, leading to localized pH reduction and chemical burns. Novel drug delivery systems, such as nanostructured floating rafts, may offer a future approach to prevent bisphosphonate-induced DEU. 38 Antibiotics (e.g. doxycycline, clindamycin) form an acidic solution when in contact with water and can cause localized ulceration without stricture formation, which typically resolves upon drug discontinuation. 39

Antineoplastic agents (e.g. fluorouracil, sunitinib) impair esophageal mucosal repair by inhibiting cell proliferation (e.g. fluorouracil interferes with DNA synthesis) and may also induce systemic immunosuppression, increasing the risk of opportunistic infections. 31 Sunitinib, a multi-targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitor, may exacerbate mucosal ischemia by inhibiting angiogenesis. 33

Immunosuppressants (e.g. tacrolimus, meclofenamic acid) reduce mucosal immune defenses by inhibiting T-cell function or purinergic synthesis, promoting opportunistic infections (e.g. cytomegalovirus) and leading to ulcer formation. 11 , 30 , 32 NSAIDs contribute to ulcer formation by reducing prostaglandin-mediated mucosal protection and causing direct cellular damage. 40 Anticoagulants (e.g. dabigatran etexilate, warfarin) may synergistically increase bleeding risk when combined with NSAIDs or glucocorticoids. 41 Patient-related factors predominantly involve those that prolong the transit time of drugs in the esophagus. 3

Age-related reductions in salivation, anatomical changes in the esophagus, taking medications at bedtime, and motor impairments may all increase esophageal transit time. 42 The most significant factor, however, is taking medications with insufficient water or while lying down. 43 To prevent drug-induced esophagitis, patients should follow medication instructions carefully: remain upright for at least 30 min after ingestion, take medications with at least 180 ml of water, and consider liquid formulations for bedridden patients or those with dysphagia. 44

However, several limitations of this study should be acknowledged. First, the spontaneous reporting nature of FAERS data may result in underreporting or overreporting. 16 – 18 FAERS accepts reports from patients and their families, which may affect the clinical accuracy of the information but also reflects patients’ real-world experiences. The FDA encourages patient reporting to capture a broader range of potential signals. Second, behavioral factors such as medication adherence and body position cannot be obtained from the database. Third, the high frequency of missing or inconsistent data in the “time-to-onset” field prevented meaningful analysis of DEU latency. This limitation underscores the hypothesis-generating nature of pharmacovigilance signals from spontaneous reports, which are better suited for identifying potential associations than for defining precise temporal patterns. Fourth, concomitant medications may act as confounding factors for DEU, and further research is needed to clarify these interactions. Serious, unusual, or highly publicized adverse events are more likely to be reported than mild or common ones, which may lead to overestimation of risk for certain drugs (e.g. newly marketed agents) and underestimation for others. Fifth, FAERS reports are heterogeneous and often lack critical clinical details, such as complete medication history, patient comorbidities, or endoscopic confirmation of ulcers, limiting the ability to control for confounding factors. A low report count does not necessarily indicate absence of risk, as many events—particularly mild ones or those attributed to other causes—may go unreported. This is a fundamental limitation of all passive surveillance systems. There may also be significant delays between the onset of an adverse event and its submission to FAERS, which can affect the timeliness of signal detection for newly marketed drugs. Disproportionality analyses identify statistical “signals” of drug-event associations reported more frequently than expected, but they cannot establish definitive causal relationships. PRR and ROR methods cannot fully eliminate confounding bias, which may introduce some degree of distortion into the results. Therefore, clinical decisions should not be made solely on these findings, though enhanced monitoring is advised. It is important to emphasize that this study is hypothesis-generating in nature and should be interpreted alongside clinical judgment and other supporting evidence. Pharmacists, with their expertise in medication management and risk mitigation, are integral members of patient safety teams and should participate in all adverse event management processes. 19 , 45 – 47 Future research should focus on validating signal strength through prospective cohort studies, investigating underlying mechanisms using esophageal mucosal biopsies and drug concentration monitoring, and developing multi-dimensional risk prediction models, potentially leveraging machine learning. Additionally, optimization of dosage forms for high-risk drugs represents a promising strategy to reduce DEU incidence.

Conclusion This large-scale pharmacovigilance study suggests that a broader spectrum of drugs may be associated with DEU than previously recognized, particularly among immunomodulating and antineoplastic agents. The findings may inform more targeted patient counseling regarding proper medication administration and highlight the need for focused monitoring in high-risk populations. These results require validation in prospective clinical studies to further clarify causality and quantify risk. Acknowledgment None.

Karger GmbH, Freiburg 2018 Background Non-cardiac chest pain (NCCP) is recurrent angina pectoris-like pain without evidence of coronary heart disease in conventional diagnostic evaluation. The prevalence of NCCP is up to 70% and may be detected (in this order) at all levels of the medical health care system (general practitioner, emergency department, chest pain unit, coronary care). Reduction of quality of life due to NCCP is comparable, and partially even higher, to that caused by cardiac chest pain. Reasons for psychological strain are symptom recurrence in approximately 50%, nonspecific diagnosis with resulting uncertainty, and insufficient integration of other medical disciplines in the diagnostic workup.

Methods and Results The management of patients with chest pain has to be multidisciplinary because non-cardiac causes may be frequently encountered. Especially gastroenterological expertise is required since the cause of chest pain is gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) in 50–60%, hypercontractile esophageal motility disorders with nutcracker/jackhammer esophagus or diffuse esophageal spasm or achalasia in 15–18%, and other esophageal alterations (e.g., infectious esophageal inflammation, drug-induced ulcers, rings, webs, eosinophilic esophagitis) in 32–35%. Conclusion This review highlights the importance of regular interdisciplinary ward rounds and management of chest pain units.

Esophageal candidiasis (EC) is the most common type of infectious esophagitis. In the gastrointestinal tract, the esophagus is the second most susceptible to candida infection, only after the oropharynx. Immunocompromised patients are most at risk, including patients with HIV/AIDS, leukemia, diabetics, and those who are receiving corticosteroids, radiation, and chemotherapy. Another group includes those who used antibiotics frequently and those who have esophageal motility disorder (cardiac achalasia and scleroderma). Patients complained of pain on swallowing, difficulty swallowing, and pain behind the sternum. On physical examination, there is a plaque that often occurs together with oral thrush. Endoscopic examination is the best approach to diagnose this disease by directly observing the white mucosal plaque-like lesions and exudates adherent to the mucosa. These adherent lesions cannot be washed off with water from irrigation. This disease is confirmed histologically by taking the biopsy or brushings of yeast and pseudohyphae invading mucosal cells. The treatment is by systemic antifungal drugs given orally in a defined course. It is important to differentiate esophageal candidiasis from other forms of infectious esophagitis such as cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, gastroesophageal reflux disease, medication-induced esophagitis, radiation-induced esophageal injury, and inflammatory conditions such as eosinophilic esophagitis.
